                                                Toric Differential Inclusions and
                                           a Proof of the Global Attractor Conjecture




arXiv:1501.02860v3 [math.DS] 23 Sep 2026
                                                               Gheorghe Craciun
                                                        Department of Mathematics and
                                                     Department of Biomolecular Chemistry
                                                       University of Wisconsin-Madison
                                                       e-mail: craciun@math.wisc.edu


                                                                       version 3.0
                                                                   September 24, 2026


                                                                           Abstract
                                            The global attractor conjecture says that toric dynamical systems have
                                            a globally attracting point (up to linear conservation relations) — or,
                                            equivalently, complex balanced systems have a globally attracting point
                                            within each stoichiometric compatibility class. A proof of this conjec-
                                            ture implies that a large class of nonlinear dynamical systems on the
                                            positive orthant have very simple and stable dynamics. The conjec-
                                            ture originates from the 1972 breakthrough work by Fritz Horn and
                                            Roy Jackson, and was formulated in its current form by Horn in 1974.
                                                 Toric dynamical systems can be embedded into toric differential
                                            inclusions. We show that each bounded positive solution of a toric
                                            differential inclusion is contained in an invariant region that prevents
                                            it from approaching the boundary of the positive orthant. We use this
                                            result to prove the global attractor conjecture. In particular, it follows
                                            that all detailed balanced mass action systems and all deficiency zero
                                            weakly reversible systems have the global attractor property.

1       Introduction
Any autonomous polynomial dynamical system1 on the strictly positive or-
thant Rn>0 can be represented as
                              dx    X
                                 =          ky→y′ xy (y ′ − y)                             (1)
                              dt   y→y ′ ∈G

for some Euclidean embedded graph2 G and some positive constants
                                                             Qn ky→y    ′,
                  3       ′                y                         yi
one for each edge y → y of G. (Here x denotes the monomial i=1 xi .)
Similarly, any non-autonomous polynomial dynamical system on Rn>0 can be
represented as
                       dx      X
                            =        ky→y′ (t)xy (y ′ − y)           (2)
                       dt        ′
                              y→y ∈G

for some nonnegative scalar functions ky→y′ (t).
    Positive trajectories of (1) and (2) are also trajectories of mass-action
systems [16]. There is great interest in understanding the persistence and
global stability properties of such dynamical systems [16, 17, 11, 12, 14, 13,
21, 22, 28, 23, 24, 25, 8, 10, 4, 20, 5, 7, 19, 3, 9, 18]. A natural question is
the following: for which systems (1) or (2) is it true that trajectories that
start in Rn>0 stay away4 from the boundary of Rn>0 ?
    Given a polynomial dynamical system, the choice of graph G above is
not unique. We will see that if the graph G can be chosen such that each
edge of G is contained in a cycle5 , then any bounded trajectory of (1) must
be persistent in Rn>0 . More generally, this is also true for solutions of (2),
provided that the nonnegative scalar functions ky→y′ (t) are bounded away
from zero and infinity6 .
    1
     or more generally any power law system [3], since we do not assume that the coor-
dinates of the vertex points y are either integer or non-negative. In particular, if vertex
points have non-negative integer coordinates we obtain mass-action systems.
   2
     A Euclidean embedded graph G is a finite directed graph whose set of vertices is
Y ⊂ Rn . See Fig. 1 for examples.
   3
     Inspired by notation from reaction networks, we denote an directed edge from y to y ′
by y → y ′ . Moreover, if y → y ′ is an edge in G we simply write y → y ′ ∈ G.
   4
     i.e., for a trajectory x(t), we have lim inf xi (t) > 0 for all i = 1, ..., n. Then we say
                                           t→∞
that the trajectory x(t) is persistent.
   5
     or, equivalently, each connected component of G is strongly connected. If this is the
case, we will say that the graph G is weakly reversible.
   6
     i.e., there exists ε > 0 such that ky→y′ (t) ∈ [ε, 1ε ] for all t.

Figure 1: Four examples of Euclidean embedded graphs in R2 . The two graphs on the right are
weakly reversible, and the bottom-right graph is reversible. Although the bottom-left graph is not weakly
reversible, it generates dynamical systems (1) which can also be represented by some weakly reversible
graph. This is not true for the top-left graph.



    In this paper we prove the results mentioned above, and use them to
prove the global attractor conjecture, which says that toric dynamical sys-
tems have a global attractor within any linear invariant subspace7 . A toric
dynamical system is a polynomial dynamical system8 for which there exists
a representation of the form (1) that admits a vertex-balanced equilibrium in
   7
      A linear invariant subspace of (1) is an invariant set S0 = (x0 + S0 ) ∩ Rn>0 , where S0
is a linear subset of Rn . For toric dynamical systems we will see that S0 = span{y ′ − y :
y → y ′ ∈ G} gives rise to a linear invariant subspace for any x0 ∈ Rn>0 .
    8
      or more generally a power law system [3].


                                                   5
Rn>0 , i.e., there exists x0 ∈ Rn>0 such that for each vertex y ∈ Y we have
                            X               X
                                 ky→y xy0 =       ky→y xy0 .                (3)
                            y→y∈G                 y→y∈G

In other words, if we think of the positive number ky→y′ xy as a flow from the
vertex y to the vertex y ′ , then condition (3) says that at each vertex of the
graph G, the sum of all the incoming flows equals the sum of all outgoing
flows. The identity (3) implies that the graph G is weakly reversible [16].
    The name “toric dynamical system” has been introduced [10] in order
to emphasize the remarkable algebraic properties of these systems, but this
class of polynomial dynamical systems has been first studied in depth in the
1972 breakthrough paper of Horn and Jackson [16], where they have been
called complex balanced mass-action systems. Also in [16] Horn and Jackson
have shown that these systems enjoy remarkable stability properties, and in
particular they have a unique positive equilibrium within each linear invari-
ant subspace, and this equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable. Actually,
in [16] Horn and Jackson stated that the unique positive equilibrium within
each linear invariant subspace is a global attractor9 , but soon afterwards Horn
explained that they have not actually proved this claim, and in 1974 he pro-
posed this global convergence property as a conjecture [17].
    The conjecture that toric dynamical systems have a global attractor within
each linear invariant subspace (or, in the language of Horn, that complex
balanced mass-action systems have a global attractor within each reaction
simplex) was later called the global attractor conjecture [10].
    The global attractor conjecture has resisted efforts for a proof for over
five decades, but proofs of many special cases have been obtained during this
time, for example [21, 22, 10, 4, 5, 19, 3, 18].
    In particular, Craciun, Nazarov and Pantea [3] have proved the three-
dimensional case, and Pantea has generalized this result for the case where
the dimension of the linear invariant subspaces is at most three [18]. Using a
different approach, Anderson has proved the conjecture under the additional
hypothesis that the graph G has a single connected component [5], and this
result has been generalized by Gopalkrishnan, Miller, and Shiu for the case
where the graph G is strongly endotactic [15].
    The results described above do not provide a proof of the global attractor
conjecture in full generality, and also do not provide a proof for any of the
   9
    i.e., if the positive equilibrium x0 belongs to the linear invariant subspace S0 , then all
trajectories that start in S0 converge to x0 .


                                              6
following three important special cases: (i) the case where G is reversible10 ,
(ii) the case where G is reversible and the system (1) is detailed balanced11 ,
and (iii) the case where G is reversible and ky→y′ = ky′ →y for all y → y ′ ∈ G.

   The goal of this paper is to use toric differential inclusions in order to
construct a proof of the global attractor conjecture in full generality.

    Toric differential inclusions are defined as follows12 . Consider a finite set
F of polyhedral cones13 that cover Rn , such that F is a polyhedral fan14
[29, 30], and fix some real number δ > 0. For each cone C ∈ F denote
by C o the polar cone15 of C. Then for each x ∈ Rn define FF ,δ (x) to be the
convex cone generated by the union of polar cones C o for all C ∈ F such that
dist(x, C) < δ. Then a toric differential inclusion is a differential inclusion
on Rn>0 given by
                                dx
                                   ∈ FF ,δ (log x).                            (4)
                                dt

    It turns out that, although the global attractor conjecture is formulated
in terms of some systems if the form (1), it will be very useful to understand
some properties of systems of the form (4) in order to construct a proof of
the conjecture. Indeed, we can “embed” some systems of the form (1) (and
even some systems of the form (2)) into toric differential inclusions:

Theorem A. If a polynomial dynamical system has a representation (2)
such that G is weakly reversible and the non-negative functions ky→y′ (t) are
  10
     i.e., if y → y ′ ∈ G then also y ′ → y ∈ G.
  11
     i.e., we replace the vertex-balance equilibrium condition (3) with the more restrictive
edge-balance equilibrium condition: ky→y xy0 = ky→y xy0 for all y → y ∈ G. This condition
says that, at the equilibrium point x0 , the “forward flux” balances the “reverse flux” for
any edge in G.
  12
     See section 4.1 for more details and examples.
  13
     A polyhedral cone in Rn is the intersection of a finite set of half-spaces of Rn .
  14
     A polyhedral fan in Rn is a finite set F of polyhedral cones such that (i) any face of
a cone in F is also in F, and (ii) the intersection of two cones in F is a face of both
cones. Simple examples of polyhedral fans FH in Rn are given by the polyhedral cones
delimited by a finite set H of hyperplanes that contain the origin. This particular case of
“hyperplane-generated polyhedral fan” is especially relevant for motivating our definition
of toric differential inclusions.
  15
     The polar cone of a cone C ∈ Rn is the cone C o = {y ∈ Rn | x·y ≤ 0 for all x ∈ C} [31].



                                             7
bounded away from zero and infinity, then it can be embedded16 in a toric
differential inclusion.

The theorem has already been proved in [2]. In particular, it follows that
if G is weakly reversible, then (1) can be embedded in a toric differential
inclusion for any choice of parameters ky→y′ > 0. We then prove that, for
any toric differential inclusion T and for any positive point x0 ∈ Rn>0 , there
exists a hypersurface H ⊂ Rn>0 that separates Rn≥0 into two regions, such that
∂Rn>0 and x0 are in different regions, and the “upper” region of H (i.e., the
region that contains the point x0 ) is at positive distance from ∂Rn>0 , and is a
forward-invariant region for the solutions of T that remain inside some cube
[0, M ]n . We will refer to this kind of hypersurface H as a zero-separating
hypersurface17 :

Theorem B. Toric differential inclusions have an exhaustive18 family of
zero-separating hypersurfaces.

Most of our effort in this paper will be spent on the proof of Theorem B.
Then we will use this result to conclude that trajectories of toric dynamical
systems must stay away from the boundary of Rn>0 :

Theorem C. Toric dynamical systems are persistent.

Finally, we will be able to conclude that the global attractor conjecture is
true:

Theorem D. Toric dynamical systems have a globally attracting point within
each positive linear invariant subspace.



  16
      We say that the dynamical system dx  dt = f (x) is embedded into the differential inclusion
dx
 dt ∈ F (x) in the domain Ω, if f (x) ∈ F (x) for all x ∈ Ω.
   17
      Note that the (fundamental) notion of “zero-separating hypersurface” here is differ-
ent from (but still very similar with) the identically-named notion of “zero-separating
hypersurface” in [1]. See section 4 for more details.
   18
      For our goals, it is not sufficient to construct a single zero-separating hypersurface;
instead we need a family of zero-separating hypersurfaces Zε such that for any x0 ∈ Rn>0
there exists some ε such that x0 is in the “upper” region of Zε . This is called an exhaustive
family of zero-separating hypersurfaces.


                                               8
2      Definitions and notation
As we mentioned in the previous section, some of the main objects of in-
terest in this paper are non-autonomous polynomial dynamical systems of
the form (2) such that the graph G is weakly reversible, and the nonnega-
tive scalar functions ky→y′ (t) are bounded away from zero and infinity. We
will refer to this class of dynamical systems as variable-k weakly reversible
dynamical systems19 .
    More precisely, a variable-k weakly reversible dynamical system is a dy-
namical system on Rn>0 of the form
                         dx     X
                            =         ky→y′ (t) xy (y ′ − y)              (5)
                         dt       ′
                               y→y ∈G

such that G is weakly reversible, and there exists a fixed positive number ε
such that ε ≤ ky→y′ (t) ≤ 1ε for all t and for all y → y ′ ∈ G.
   Note that, under these conditions, solutions of the variable-k weakly re-
versible dynamical system above are also solutions of the differential inclusion
on Rn>0 given by
                               (                                            )
  dx                               X                                      1
      ∈ F (x), where F (x) =             ky→y′ xy (y ′ − y) | ε ≤ ky→y′ ≤     .
  dt                                  ′
                                 y→y ∈G
                                                                          ε
                                                                                 (6)
    We will show that solutions of the differential inclusion (6) are also solu-
tions of a type of differential inclusions with rich geometric properties, called
toric differential inclusions. Later in this section we will define the general
notion of toric differential inclusions in Rn>0 . We first define the class of polar
differential inclusions in Rn .

2.1     Polar differential inclusions
If the graph G is reversible, then the equations (5) can be written as
              dx      X                                ′
                                                          
                  =           ky→y′ (t)xy − ky′ →y (t)xy (y ′ − y),                   (7)
              dt     y⇌y ′ ∈G

  19
     Variable-k weakly reversible dynamical systems have also been called variable-k toric
dynamical systems [1], because any such dynamical system can be obtained from a toric
dynamical system by using the same graph G, and replacing the constants ky→y′ with
time-dependent non-negative functions ky→y′ (t) that are bounded away from zero and
infinity.

                                            9
by grouping together terms given by an edge y → y ′ and its reverse y ′ → y.
Then, for each reversible edge y ⇌ y ′ ∈ G, there is now a single term
in the sum (7), which can be thought of as a “tug-of-war” between the
forward and reverse terms. Indeed, both the forward and the reverse terms
are trying to “push” the state x(t) of the system along the same line20 , but
in opposite directions. Then, the domain Rn>0 can be partitioned into three
                                                           ′
regions: the region where the inequality εxy ≥ 1ε xy holds (which implies
                          ′                                                ′
ky→y′ (t)xy ≥ ky′ →y (t)xy ), the region where the inequality 1ε xy ≤ εxy holds
                                          ′
(which implies ky→y′ (t)xy ≤ ky′ →y (t)xy ), and an uncertainty region where
neither one of these two inequalities are satisfied, and either one of the two
                                   ′
terms ky→y′ (t)xy and ky′ →y (t)xy may win the tug-of-war, due to the fact that
ky→y′ (t) and ky′ →y (t) may take any values between ε and 1ε . Some concrete
examples can be found in Section 3 of [3]. In particular, note that if one term
does win the tug-of-war, then the direction of the sum of the two terms is
                                                                                 ′
towards the uncertainty region, and also towards the hypersurface xy = xy
in Rn>0 .
    The simplest way to understand how these regions adjoin each other is
to look at them in Rn instead of Rn>0 , after applying a logarithmic transfor-
                                                                    ′
mation. If we denote X = log x, then the hypersurface xy = xy becomes the
hyperplane (y ′ −y)·X = 0. Moreover, the uncertainty region described above
                                                   2|log ε|
becomes just the set of points at distance < δ = ||y  ′ −y|| from this hyperplane.
                                                    ′
Note also that the direction given by the vector y − y is exactly the direction
orthogonal to the hyperplane (y ′ − y) · X = 0.
    Therefore, if the graph G consists of a single reversible edge y ⇌ y ′ , then
the dynamics of the system (7) at a point x can be described as follows: we
know that x will move along a line of support vector (y ′ − y), and we are able
to specify one direction or another by mapping x to X = log x, and checking
whether the distance between X and the hyperplane (y ′ − y) · X = 0 is ≥ δ.
Moreover, if we can specify this direction, then it is always the direction
towards (and not away from) this hyperplane, and orthogonal to it.
    This characterization has the advantage that it can be carried over to the
more general case, where G contains several reversible edges. In that case we
have several tug-of-wars going on at the same time, but for each one of them
we can specify the winning direction (if any) at x by calculating the distance
between X = log x and some hyperplane in Rn . Depending on whether X
falls outside an uncertainty region or not, each reversible edge y ⇌ y ′ of G
  20
       i.e., a line whose direction is given by the vector y ′ − y.


                                                 10
contributes one or two resultant vectors (if one, then it is either y ′ − y or
y − y ′ , and if two, then they are ±(y ′ − y)).
    If follows that any system (7) can be embedded into a differential inclusion
on Rn>0 given by a set H of hyperplanes in Rn and a number δ > 0, as follows.
For each x ∈ Rn>0 we define FH,δ (log x) to be the convex cone generated by
vectors orthogonal to the hyperplanes of H, in the direction that goes from
the point X = log x towards each hyperplane, and also the opposite direction
if X is at distance < δ from some hyperplane. If X does not belong to any
uncertainty region, then FH,δ (log x) is defined to be exactly the polar cone
C o of a cone C bounded by a subset of hyperplanes21 from H. Moreover, if X
does belong to some uncertainty regions, then we can still describe FH,δ (log x)
in terms of polar cones, by including not just the polar of the largest cone
of F(H) that contains X, but also the polar of each cone of F(H) that is at
distance ≤ δ from X.
    Of course, not all polyhedral fans are determined by a set of hyperplanes
as above. Nevertheless, we can generalize the construction described above
to define polar differential inclusions given by a polyhedral fan F in Rn ,
as described in the previous section: we define FF ,δ (X) to be the convex
cone generated by the union of polar cones C o for all C ∈ F such that
dist(X, C) < δ.

2.2     Toric differential inclusions
Polar differential inclusions can produce sets of cones that contain the right-
hand-side of the vector fields (5) for reversible G, but they are defined on Rn ,
while the system (5) is defined on Rn>0 . To obtain a proper embedding we
need to introduce toric differential inclusions, which are obtained from polar
differential inclusions by a logarithmic transformation: a toric differential
inclusion given by a polyhedral fan F in Rn is a differential inclusion on Rn>0
given by
                                dx
                                    ∈ FF ,δ (log x)                          (8)
                                 dt
where FF ,δ is a polar differential inclusion as defined above.
    Due to the way this definition is related to the system (7), it follows that
variable-k weakly reversible dynamical systems (5) that are generated by a
  21
   the cone C is the largest cone that contains the point X within the polyhedral fan
F(H) determined by the set of hyperplanes H. The convex cone generated by the “outer
normal” vectors orthogonal to the hyperplane faces of C is its polar cone C o [30].


                                         11
reversible graph G can be embedded into polar differential inclusions.
    As we discussed above, for a reversible graph G, the polyhedral fan F
could be chosen simply as the fan generated by the set of hyperplanes that
are orthogonal to the vectors y ′ − y for y → y ′ ∈ G.
    We need to remove this strong assumption of reversibility, in order to be
able to address the global attractor conjecture in full generality. In the next
section we explain how to find such a polyhedral fan for any weakly reversible
graph G.


3      Embedding of variable-k weakly reversible
       dynamical systems into toric differential in-
       clusions
As we discussed in the previous section, the simplest examples of polar differ-
ential inclusions are generated by polyhedral fans FH that are determined by
a finite set H of hyperplanes22 that pass through the origin. Then, the sim-
plest examples of toric differential inclusions are also generated by polyhedral
fans FH as above. We will refer to this class of toric differential inclusions as
hyperplane-generated toric differential inclusions.
    We have seen in the previous section that any reversible variable-k weakly
reversible dynamical system in Rn>0 can be embedded into a (hyperplane-
generated) toric differential inclusion. Here we show that a similar fact is
true for all variable-k weakly reversible dynamical systems23 .

Theorem 3.1. Consider a variable-k weakly reversible dynamical system (5).
Then this system can be embedded into a toric differential inclusion.

Proof. This theorem has already been proved in [2]. We discuss a sketch of
the proof below, see [2] for more details.
    Assume first that the weakly reversible graph G is made up of a single
directed cycle. If our single-cycle graph is given by y1 → y2 → ... → yr → y1 ,
  22
     i.e., FH consists of all the cones delimited by hyperplanes in H.
  23
     In order to prove the global attractor conjecture we plan to construct some forward-
invariant sets for any given toric dynamical system (not just for the reversible ones).
Theorem 3.1 will help us argue that we can accomplish our goal by constructing something
called zero-separating surfaces (ZSH) for toric differential inclusions.



                                           12
then the variable-k weakly reversible dynamical system it generates is of the
form                           r
                        dx X
                           =      ki (t) xyi (yi+1 − yi ),                (9)
                        dt    i=1

where yr+1 = y1 and ε0 ≤ ki (t) ≤ ε10 for some ε0 > 0.
     Consider the set L of lines through the origin in the direction of vectors
yi − yj for all i ̸= j, and denote by H the set of all hyperplanes that are
orthogonal complements of lines in L24 . Denote by FH the polyhedral fan
generated by the set of hyperplanes H, and, for δ > 0, denote by TH,δ the
corresponding hyperplane-generated toric differential inclusion. We will show
that there exists δ0 > 0 such that the single-cycle variable-k weakly reversible
dynamical system (9) is embedded in the toric differential inclusion TH,δ0 .
     Choose δ0 > 0 large enough such that the uncertainty regions given by
the reversible edges yi ⇌ yj and ε0 are contained within the uncertainty
regions of the toric differential inclusion TH,δ0 .
     Fix a point x ∈ Rn>0 such that X = log x belongs to some cone C in
FH , and does not belong to any uncertainty region of TH,δ0 . In particular, it
follows that the cone C has dimension n, otherwise X would be contained in
some hyperplane in H, which in turn would be contained in an uncertainty
region of TH,δ0 . We want to show that the right-hand-side of (9) is contained
in the dual cone C o .
     Consider a vector w in the interior of C, and project y1 , y2 , ..., yr on the
line lw that passes through the origin in the direction given by w. Then no two
projections are the same, because w does not belong to any of the hyperplanes
in H. We now give a second set of names to the vectors y1 , y2 , ..., yr , say
v1 , v2 , ..., vr , to record the distance to the origin of the projections along the
line (i.e., if the projection of yi1 is the closest to origin, then v1 = yi1 , and if
the projection of yi2 is the second closest to origin, then v2 = yi2 , and so on).
Note that, since the interior of C is disjoint from all the hyperplanes in H, it
follows that the new names v1 , v2 , ..., vr do not depend on the particular choice
of vector w in the interior of C. In other words, the dot products (vl+1 −vl )·w
are all negative numbers, for all w in the interior of C. Therefore, the vectors
v2 − v1 , v3 − v2 , ..., vr − vr−1 belong to C o .
     So, in order to show that the right-hand side of (9) is included in C o , it
is enough to show that it can be written as a positive linear combination of
the vectors v2 − v1 , v3 − v2 , ..., vr − vr−1 .
  24
       i.e., a hyperplane belongs to H iff it is orthogonal to a line in L.


                                                13
    Note that (i1 , i2 , ..., ir ) is a permutation of (1, 2, ..., r). If we denote the
inverse permutation by (j1 , j2 , ..., jr ), it follows that y1 = vj1 , y2 = vj2 , and
so on.
    Then we have y2 − y1 = vj2 − vj1 . If j2 > j1 we write

and if j2 < j1 we write
                                            j1 −1

                                            l=j2

We do the same for y3 − y2 , y4 − y3 , and so on. This way, we write each
difference yi+1 − yi from the right-hand-side of (9) in terms of the vectors
±(yl+1 − yl ), with l = 1, 2, ..., r − 1. Therefore we can re-group terms to
obtain
                                    r−1

where Φl is a sum of several terms of the form ki xvi , with various signs.
    Note now that the positive terms inside Φl correspond to edges of the form
vm → vn with m ≤ l < n, and negative terms inside Φl correspond to edges
of the form vm → vn with n ≤ l < m. This means that the positive terms
inside Φl contain ki xvi with i ≤ l, and the negative terms inside Φl contain
ki xvi with i > l. Since log x ∈ C (and is not in an uncertainty region), and
due to our choice of δ0 , it follows that k1 xv1 < k2 xv2 < ... < kr xvr . Therefore,
the sum of the positive terms inside Φl dominates the sum of the negative
terms inside Φl , for each l25 . In conclusion, the right-hand-side of (10) (and
therefore (9)) is a positive linear combination of the vectors vl+1 − vl , for
1 ≤ l ≤ r − 1, so it belongs to C o .

    If x does belong to an uncertainty region of the toric differential inclusion
TH,δ0 , then denote by F (x) the cone of TH,δ0 at x. It follows that the maximal
linear subspace contained in F (x) has dimension ≥ 1 in Rn . We project the
problem on the orthogonal complement of that subspace, and then we reason

                                           15
4    Strategy for the proof of the global attrac-
     tor conjecture: the big picture

In order to prove the global attractor conjecture we will prove that toric
dynamical systems are persistent. It has been known for a long time that
persistence of toric dynamical systems, together with a simple application of
the LaSalle invariance principle would immediately imply global stability [21,
22, 32].
    More precisely, we will prove the following stronger fact: for any positive
initial condition x0 ∈ Rn>0 of a toric dynamical system there exists a compact
forward invariant region Kx0 ⊂ Rn>0 such that x0 ∈ Kx0 . Of course, this
implies that toric dynamical systems are persistent.
    In order to accomplish this goal, our main focus will be the construction of
a specific type of hypersurfaces in Rn>0 called zero-separating hypersurfaces (ZSH),
which, when considered together with well-chosen level sets of the Horn-
Jackson Lyapunov function, give rise to compact forward invariant regions
Kx0 like we mentioned above; see Figure 2 for a two-dimensional example (in
this example the ZSH is just a curve).
    More precisely, our strategy will be to construct polyhedral zero-separating
hypersurfaces (polyhedral ZSH). Our construction of a polyhedral ZSH will
rely on a ZSH blueprint. A ZSH blueprint is a structure associated to a given
polyhedral fan, which contains inside complete instructions for the construc-
tion of an exhaustive family of ZSH. Polyhedral fans are relevant because
of the theorem on embedding toric dynamical systems into toric differen-
tial inclusions; and a toric differential inclusion (denoted TF ,δ ) is given by a
polyhedral fan F and a positive number δ.
    In our construction of polyhedral ZSH we will see that the specific number
δ above will practically become irrelevant, and it will turn out that we will
not need to look in much depth at detailed properties of toric differential
inclusions; it will be sufficient to focus almost exclusively on the much simpler
notion of polyhedral fan.
    Therefore, given a polyhedral fan F, we will develop a step-by-step pro-
cess that allows us to construct some polyhedral hypersurfaces associated to
F. More precisely, we will show how to construct such families of polyhedral
hypersurfaces by taking advantage of a ZSH blueprint, and we will see later
that these hypersurfaces are indeed zero-separating hypersurfaces.


                                      16
In summary, we will proceed according to the following plan28 :
    Step 0. Given a toric dynamical system Tn+1 in Rn+1   >0 , we embed it into
a toric differential inclusion Tn+1 , generated by a polyhedral fan Fn+1 and a
number δ > 0.
    Step 1. Given the polyhedral fan Fn+1 in Rn+1 we construct the x1 -xn -
subdivision Sn of Rn generated by Fn+1 .
    Step 2. Given the x1 -xn -subdivision Sn we construct a ZSH blueprint Bn
for Sn .
    Step 3. Given the ZSH blueprint Bn we construct an exhaustive family of
n-dimensional polyhedral ZSHs denoted Zε in Rn+1   >0 .
                                            n+1
    Step 4. We show that for any x0 ∈ R>0 there exists a polyhedral hyper-
surface Zε among the ones that we have constructed in step 3, such that Zε
(together with a well-chosen level set of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov func-
tion) determines a compact set Kx0 ⊂ Rn+1  >0 such that x0 ∈ Kx0 and Kx0 is a
forward invariant region for the toric dynamical system Tn+1 that we started
with in Step 0.
    Step 0 has already been done in [2], and we have discussed it in section 3.
Step 1 will not be difficult, but we will need to we restrict our attention
(without loss of generality) to x1 -xn+1 -fans. Steps 2 and 3 are very much
interconnected, and most of our effort will focus on these two steps. Step 4
will be a relatively quick corollary of the previous steps.

4.1     Polyhedral fans and toric differential inclusions
In this subsection we revisit some definitions and results that have also been
mentioned in a previous section, and we look at a few simple examples that
illustrate these notions. The reader who is familiar with the notions and
results from the previous sections can skip this subsection.
Definition 4.1. A polyhedral fan in Rn is a finite collection F of closed
convex polyhedral cones29 in Rn ,

                                   F = {C1 , ..., Cm },
  28
      For convenience of notation we assume that we start in (n + 1)-dimensional space;
then the fundamentals steps (i.e., Steps 2 and 3) take place in n-dimensional space.
   29
      All the cones we are interested in here are closed convex polyhedral cones; therefore,
from now on, whenever we say “cone”, we mean “closed convex polyhedral cone”.


                                            17
Figure 2: A two-dimensional illustration of the interplay between the ZSH (the blue curve) and a well
chosen level set of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function (the orange curve), such that together they give
rise to a compact forward invariant region (the green region).



such that we have
   (i) for any cone Ci ∈ F any face of Ci also belongs to F,
and
   (ii) for any Ci , Cj ∈ F their intersection Ci ∩ Cj is a common face of
both of them.

    We say that the polyhedral fan F is pointed if any cone C ∈ F is a pointed
cone. Also, we say that a polyhedral fan F in Rn is complete if the union of
all the cones in F is the whole Rn .
    Here we are only interested in pointed and complete polyhedral fans, and
for simplicity we will refer to them simply as fans (in other words, from
now on whenever we say “fan”, we mean “pointed and complete polyhedral
fan”)30 .
    See Figure 3(a) for an illustration of a fan in R2 . This fan consists of 13
cones: six cones of dimension 2, six cones of dimension 1, and one cone of
dimension 0 (i.e., the origin of R2 ).

Definition 4.2. Given a fan F and a real number δ > 0 we define the
toric differential inclusion generated by F and δ as follows. For any x ∈
Rn>0 we consider all the cones Cj ∈ F such that dist(log x, Cj ) < δ and
define FF ,δ (x) to be the cone generated by the union of all polar cones Cj◦ .
  30
    In some instances we will need to refer to the set of all the cones of a fan F that are
contained in a specific subset of Rn ; in this case we will say “restricted fan”.



                                                 18
Then the toric differential inclusion generated by F and δ is given by
                                      dx
                                         ∈ FF ,δ (x).                                   (11)
                                      dt

    For example, in the case of the fan F2 shown in Figure 3(a), we can see
that the right-hand side of the corresponding toric differential inclusion (i.e.,
FF2 ,δ (x)) consists of a piecewise constant choice of convex cones (one for each
Cj ∈ F2 ), as shown in Figure 3(c).

    Toric differential inclusions are useful in the study of the global attractor
conjecture because of the following embedding theorem [2], which implies
that one can reduce the problem of building forward-invariant regions for
toric dynamical systems to the analogous problem for toric differential inclu-
sions.

Theorem 4.3. Consider a variable-k weakly reversible31 dynamical system.
Then this dynamical system can be embedded into a toric differential inclu-
sion. More precisely, if our variable-k weakly reversible dynamical system is
given by
                                 dx
                                    = f (t, x),
                                 dt
then there exists a fan F and some δ > 0 such that we have

                                    f (t, x) ∈ FF ,δ (x),

for all t ∈ R and all x ∈ Rn>0 .

4.2     Forward invariant regions and ZSH for toric dif-
        ferential inclusions
We are interested in constructing forward-invariant regions for toric differen-
tial inclusions. Let us first define the following notion:
  31
    Note that toric dynamical systems are special cases of weakly reversible systems; in
particular, every toric dynamical system has a fixed vector of parameters (i.e., reaction rate
constants) k, but not every weakly reversible system with a fixed vector of parameters is
a toric dynamical system (because, in general, the “vertex balance condition” is sufficient
but not necessary for weak reversibility).



                                             19
Definition 4.4. Consider a piecewise smooth surface Z in Rn>0 , and a toric
differential inclusion T in Rn>0 generated by a fan F and a number δ > 0. If
P is a smooth point of Z, we say that T cannot cross Z at P if the tangent
hyperplane of Z at P is a supporting hyperplane of the cone FF ,δ (P ). Also,
for a set Ω ∈ Rn>0 , we say that T cannot cross Z within Ω if T cannot cross
Z at any smooth point P ∈ Ω.
   Let us note the following simple characterization of the condition that T
cannot cross Z at P :
Remark 4.5. Consider a piecewise smooth surface Z in Rn>0 , and a toric
differential inclusion T in Rn>0 generated by a fan F and a number δ > 0.
Consider a smooth point of Z denoted P . Then T cannot cross Z at P if
and only if there exists a normal vector ⃗nP of Z at P such that ⃗nP ∈ C for
any cone C ∈ F that satisfies the condition
                                   dist(C, log P ) < δ.
    Indeed, this follows immediately from the definition of the cone FF ,δ (P )
in (11), together with the general observation that the cone generated by
a union of polar cones equals the polar cone of the intersection of those
cones [31].

    The key notion in this section is the zero-separating hypersurface, or ZSH
for short:
Definition 4.6. Consider a piecewise smooth surface Z in Rn>0 , and a toric
differential inclusion T in Rn>0 generated by a fan F and a number δ > 0.
We say that Z is a zero-separating hypersurface for T (or Z is ZSH for T )
if the following are true:
    (i) there exists some η ∈ (0, 1) such that
                                 Z ⊂ Rn>0 \ (η + Rn>0 ),
   (ii) Z intersects every toric ray32 in Rn>0 exactly once,
and
   (iii) there exists some M ≥ 1 such that the toric differential inclusion T
cannot cross Z within the set (0, M )n .
  32
    A toric ray in Rn is the image via the exponential function of a line that passes through
the origin of Rn . Note that every toric ray is contained in Rn>0 and passes through the
point of coordinates (1, 1, . . . , 1) ∈ Rn>0 .


                                             20
    Recall that, given a toric differential inclusion T in Rn>0 , we want to con-
struct a family of ZSH for T denoted Zε such that each such ZSH (together
with a well-chosen level set of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function) gives
rise to a compact forward invariant set Kε ⊂ Rn>0 for the toric dynamical
system that we have started with. Moreover, we want to make sure that for
any initial state x0 ∈ Rn>0 there is some ε such that x0 ∈ Kε . Then, as we
mentioned before, we obtain a proof of the global attractor conjecture.

    Indeed, see Figure 2 for an illustration in R2>0 . More concretely, if we
think of the blue polyhedral line in Figure 2 as a ZSH denoted Zε , we will
want the polyhedral line Zε to get closer and closer to the axes of the positive
quadrant as ε gets closer and closer to zero; at the same time, we will want the
orange curve (which is a level curve of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function
in R2>0 ) to move farther and farther away, so the green forward-invariant
region grows bigger and bigger, such that any x0 ∈ R2>0 will be contained to
such a green region. In other words, we want the polyhedral lines Zε to form
an exhaustive family of ZSHs.




                                       21
5     Proof of the global attractor conjecture in
      the two-dimensional case.
In this section we discuss the proof of the two-dimensional global attractor
conjecture, by relying on two-dimensional toric differential inclusions.
    Recall that the two-dimensional global attractor conjecture has first been
proved in [4], without the use of toric differential inclusions; but, due to the
relevance of toric differential inclusions in our proof of the n-dimensional
global attractor conjecture we will focus here on how two-dimensional toric
differential inclusions can be used in the proof of the two-dimensional global
attractor conjecture. Our main interest is to illustrate the use of toric dif-
ferential inclusions (and especially polyhedral fans ) in such a proof, where
several important aspects of a rich geometric structure of the problem be-
come important, and easy to see.

5.1    Construction of ZSH for two-dimensional toric dif-
       ferential inclusions
Two-dimensional toric differential inclusions admit ZSHs that are polygonal
curves, such as the blue curve in Figure 3(d). Note that if this curve is
constructed close enough to boundary of the positive quadrant then it does
not visit the more complicated regions in the middle of the figure. Therefore,
in order to construct such a ZSH it is sufficient for us to focus on the right-
hand side of the toric differential inclusion near the boundary of the positive
quadrant.
    We can see in Figure 3(d) that the (explicitly specified) cones of the toric
differential inclusion can be used in order to construct a polygonal curve that
cannot be crossed by solutions of toric differential inclusions, and therefore
cannot be crossed by solutions of a toric dynamical system that is embedded
in this toric differential inclusion (this is discussed in detail in [2]).
    More precisely, we can see in Figure 3(e) that the blue polygonal line can
be used together with an level set of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function
(the orange curve) to create a forward invariant region that allows us to
conclude immediately (using the LaSalle invariance principle [21, 22, 32])
that the global convergence property holds for any solution with initial value
inside this region. In other words, the blue polygonal curve is a ZSH.
    If we choose some initial point x0 ∈ R2>0 that is not in this region, then


                                      22
another such forward invariant region can be constructed that contains this
x0 , as follows. First we construct another blue polygonal curve, much closer
to the boundary of the positive quadrant. This not only ensures that x0 lies
above this curve, but also ensures that the curve can be extended farther up,
and farther to the right33 ; then we can also intersect it with a level set of
the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function that lies above the point x0 , and obtain
another forward invariant region that is now guaranteed to contain x0 .
Therefore we can conclude the desired global stability result in full generality.


5.2     A different approach: the use of a ZSH blueprint
        and representations of a fan using subdivisions
In preparation for the higher dimensional cases, we will now discuss a differ-
ent point of view for the construction of a ZSH in R2>0 , which is similar with
the approach shown in Figure 3(d), but emphasizes less the two-dimensional
fan; instead, we introduce two (equivalent) notions of subdivisions induced by
the fan, which (in this case) are one-dimensional objects that already contain
all the relevant information about the two-dimensional fan, see Figures 3(i)
and 3(j). Then, to any subdivision we associate a ZSH blueprint (see Fig-
ure 3(k)), and we use it as a essential tool that guides our construction of
the ZSH. (The ZSH constructed this way will still be a polygonal curve, but
we only need to construct it within the set {0 < x2 ≤ x1 } because we can
then infer the missing half by symmetry, see Figure 3(h).)
    Note that, compared to the simplicity of the approach we used in the previ-
ous subsection, our approach in this subsection will appear unnecessarily complicated.
This is actually true, but, as we mentioned before, our goal in this subsection
is not just to construct the ZSH in the two-dimensional case, but to go through
each and every step of the more complicated construction that we have to per-
form in higher dimensions, while we are still in the simplest nontrivial setting:
the two-dimensional case.
  33
    Note that when we extend the blue curve up or to the right within some uncertainty
region for large values of x1 or x2 , then it does not satisfy the ZSH property with that
uncertainty region. But, if we construct it closer to the boundary of the positive quadrant
then we can extended it while preserving the ZSH property farther up and farther to the
right.

    Finally, the last edge of our ZSH starts at P56 and goes in a direction or-
thogonal to the basepoint of T6 ; but the basepoint of T6 is the point at infinity
denoted Q∞ , which means that this last edge must be perfectly horizontal41 .
    To see that we have indeed succeeded in constructing a ZSH we claim
now that we are in the setting of Lemma 9.7, i.e., for any nonzero cone C in
F2≤ , the polygonal curve we have constructed above has the property that
there exists a cone KC such that C is contained in the interior of KC and such
that for any point P of the ZSH such that log(P ) belongs to KC we have that
the outer normal of the ZSH at P belongs to C.
    Indeed, if C is a one-dimensional cone in F2≤ then the image of C within
D2P is the basepoint of a tile Ti . Then we can define KC to be the two-
dimensional cone that corresponds to the tile Ti . Also, consider the case
where C is a two-dimensional cone in F2≤ . Then, regarded within D2P , the
cone C “spans” two adjacent tiles, say Ti and Ti+1 , and we can define KC to
be the two-dimensional cone that corresponds to the union of the tiles Ti and
Ti+1 .
    Note also that we can choose the initial point (ε, ε) to have an arbitrarily
small ε. Therefore, we are indeed in the setting of Lemma 9.742 , which implies
that our polygonal curve is a ZSH.




  41
     Because, informally speaking, the coordinates of Q∞ in D1P are (1, ∞). If we want to
avoid dealing with “∞” we can use the version of Q∞ from D1H (see Figure 3(i)) instead
of the Q∞ from D1P ; that one is simply the vector (0,1) so, of course, orthogonal to it
means perfectly horizontal.
  42
     Note that Lemma 9.7 only guarantees that our toric differential inclusion cannot cross
our polygonal curve within the unit square (0, 1)2 . Nevertheless, it is sufficient for our
purposes, because this will remain true for a large enough distance outside the unit square
(more precisely, until the curve reaches a new uncertainly region along one of the axes,
which, if ε is small enough, will only happen for very large values of x1 ), see Figure 3(e).


                                             28
6     Proof of the global attractor conjecture in
      the three-dimensional case
We now discuss the construction of ZSH for three-dimensional toric differen-
tial inclusions.
     For our construction of ZSH in R3>0 we will rely very heavily on two-
dimensional representations of three-dimensional fans using subdivisions of
the sets D2P (and/or D2H ) described below, and on the corresponding notion
of two-dimensional ZSH blueprint.
     Recall that in the previous section we have been able to use one-dimensional
ZSH blueprints for the construction of one-dimensional ZSH in R2>0 (i.e., for
the construction of polygonal curves that satisfy the ZSH property). More-
over, our construction was “canonical”, in the following sense: once we spec-
ified the starting point P0 of coordinates (ε, ε), everything else was uniquely
determined by the following simple conditions: (i) the edges of the ZSH are
in one-to-one correspondence with the tiles of the ZSH blueprint, (ii) each
edge is orthogonal to the basepoint of its corresponding tile, and (iii) the
image of each edge via the map Ψ2 is exactly its corresponding tile.
     In the next subsection we will choose an especially convenient fan F3 ,
define a ZSH blueprint for it, and devise a construction process for the ZSH
which is based on this ZSH blueprint. We will see that we have to adapt
and modify some of the rules (i)-(iii) described above, but in the end we
can create such a construction process, and to some extent it can also be
seen as “canonical”, under somewhat relaxed restrictions. More precisely,
our construction give rise to a polyhedral ZSH such that: (i′ ) the faces of the
ZSH are in one-to-one correspondence with the tiles of the ZSH blueprint,
(ii′ ) each face is orthogonal to the basepoint of its corresponding tile, and (iii′ )
the image of each edge via the map Ψ3 is arbitrarily close to its corresponding
tile (in a sense that will be clarified below).
     In a later subsection we will describe the construction of a polyhedral
ZSH for a fully general choice of fan F3 .




                                        29
6.1     The proof in a special case
Similar to the previous section, we consider a fan F3 that is X1 -X2 -X3 -
symmetric, and we assume43 that all planes {Xi = Xj } and {Xi = 0} can
be realized as unions of cones that belong to F3 . Recall that we only need
to specify F3 within the negative orthant; moreover, due to symmetry, we
only need to specify F3 within the subset of the negative orthant where
we have X3 ≤ X2 ≤ X1 ≤ 0. Let us denote the restriction of F3 to this
subset by F3≤ (here the superscript “≤” is meant to remind us the inequality
X3 ≤ X2 ≤ X1 ≤ 0). Then the part of F3 within the negative orthant is
uniquely determined by F3≤ , and for now on we will focus on F3≤ .
    Also similar to the previous section, the information within F3≤ is com-
pletely determined if we specify the polygonal subdivision44 F2H of D2H , ob-
tained by considering the sets of the form

                                       (−Ci ) ∩ D2H

for all the cones Ci ∈ F3≤ , where

D2H = {(X1H , X2H , X3H ) ∈ R3≥0 | X1H ≤ X2H ≤ X3H and X1H +X2H +X3H = 1}45 .

    Analogously, the information within F3≤ is completely determined if we
specify the polygonal subdivision F2P of D2P , obtained by considering the sets
of the form
                                (−Ci ) ∩ D2P
  43
     Recall that these assumptions can be made without loss of generality, because, if
needed, we are just replacing F3 with a finer version of F3 ; any ZSH for the finer fan will
also be a ZSH for the coarser fan.
  44
     By polygonal subdivision (or simply subdivision) of D2H we mean a set of convex poly-
gons, line segments, and points, which satisfies properties that are similar to the properties
of a fan: any face of an element of the subdivision is also an element of the subdivision,
and the intersection of two elements of the subdivision is a face of both.
  45
     The best way to think about the role/meaning of D2H is geometrically: D2H is a
concrete representation of the set of rays (i.e., one-dimensional cones) contained in the set
{X3 ≤ X2 ≤ X1 ≤ 0}. The element of D2H that represents a specific ray ℓ is the point
(−ℓ) ∩ D2H . This also allows us to understand why it is natural to “see” the nonzero cones
of F3≤ inside D2H : each such cone is a set of rays, so each such cone is determined by a
subset of D2H .

that are parallel to one specific half-line; equivalently, each point at infinity
corresponds to a specific slope that can be realized by half-lines contained
within D2P . Then, literally, parallel half-lines “meet at infinity” within D2P .

      3D fan F3 , whose representation as a subdivision F2P of D2P is shown in (a). In (b) we show together F2P

          Let us now clarify the notion of ZSH blueprint for this example. In gen-
      eral, given a subdivision F2P of D2P , a ZSH blueprint B(F2P ) is another subdi-
      vision of D2P into quadrilateral “tiles”, together with the choice of a preferred
      point within each tile, called the “basepoint” of the tile, which satisfies several
      additional properties. To obtain the ZSH blueprint shown in Figure 4(b) we
      have done the following:
          Step 1. We created the blue box shown with thick blue dashed lines in
      Figure 4(d), such that all the bounded49 vertices of F2P (i.e., the nine red
        49
         F2P also has two “unbounded vertices”, i.e., vertices that lie at infinity; these will be
      addressed in Step 4.


                                                         32
dots) are contained in the interior of this blue box. Note that the choice of
blue box depends just on two numbers: a large enough value of X3P where
the vertical side of the box lies, and a large enough value of X2P where the
horizontal side of the blue box lies.
    Step 2. We took advantage of the fact that the bounded vertices (i.e., the
red dots) of F2P lie along horizontal lines, and we drew the two blue horizontal
line segments that separate rows of vertices of F2P within the blue box, see
Figure 4(e).
    Step 3. We drew the six blue vertical line segments such that they com-
pletely separate the nine vertices of F2P within nine different tiles inside the
blue box, see Figure 4(f ). Also, we chose each such vertex to be the basepoint
of its corresponding tile.
    Step 4. For the region of D2P that lies outside the blue box, we drew the
three thin dashed half-lines that give rise to two additional quadrilateral tiles
“near infinity”. (These three thin dashed half-lines can be seen most clearly
in Figure 4(c).) The slope of the middle dashed half-line is chosen such that
its support line passes through the origin. Note that these two tiles also need
to have basepoints; we chose these two basepoints to lie at infinity, and to
correspond to the slopes of the half-lines of F2P within those tiles. (We are
showing these two points at infinity symbolically in Figure 4(c).)

6.1.2    The use of the ZSH blueprint B(F2P ) in the construction of
         the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P ))
After we have constructed the ZSH blueprint B(F2P ) shown in Figure 4(c), we
will use it for the construction of a polyhedral surface (denoted P(B(F2P )))
within the set where 0 < x3 ≤ x2 ≤ x1 ≤ 1.
    Later we will argue that, when we also take into account its symmetric
images (and also extend it outside the unit cube, in a way that will also be
specified later), the surface P(B(F2P )) will give rise to a ZSH for F3 .
    Our plan is that the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P )) will have 11 faces,
which will be in a one-to-one correspondence with the tiles of B(F2P ). More-
over, each face will be orthogonal to the basepoint of its corresponding tile.
Even more, the image of each face via the map ΨP3 will approximate “arbi-
trarily closely”50 its corresponding tile (see Figure 5(e) for an illustration of
  50
    We will see that, while for each face of the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P )) we can impose
that it is exactly orthogonal to the basepoint of its corresponding tile, we cannot actually


                                            33
this approximation).
    Before we start to describe the details of this construction, let us make the
following general comment: while the construction of the polyhedral surface
P(B(F2P )) takes place in R3>0 , we plan to observe our progress and collect
information about construction rules by looking at the image via

                                ΨP3 : P(B(F2P )) → D2P

of each piece of the surface while we are constructing it, and we will compare
this image to the ZSH blueprint that we already have available to us within
D2P .

    Let us “zoom-in” in the lower-left corner of Figure 4(c), which is shown
in Figure 5(a).
    We will now focus just on the regions (tiles) T1 , T2 , T3 , T4 , T5 , that are
shown in Figure 5(a). Recall that each tile Ti contains exactly one red point,
which is the basepoint of the tile.
    We now explain in detail how we can use the information present in
Figure 5(a) in order to construct the corresponding faces F1 , F2 , F3 , F4 , F5 of
the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P )), such that each face Fi corresponds to a
tile Ti in Figure 5(a). See Figure 5(b) for an informal representation of the
faces F1 , F2 , F3 , F4 , F5 in R3 . (The adjacency information in Figure 5(b) is
correct, but the faces are not shown to scale).

    Before we begin the construction of the faces Fi , let us first explain a very
convenient abuse of terminology with respect to the tiles Ti . If a vertex Q of
a tile Ti lies on the boundary of another tile Tj , we will say that Q is also
a vertex of Tj . In other words, even though all tiles are actually quadrilat-
erals, we convene that some tiles may have more than four vertices (i.e., we
regard some of these quadrilaterals as degenerate pentagons, or degenerate
hexagons, etc., in the sense that some of their vertices are degenerate, i.e.,
the interior angle at such a vertex is exactly 180o ). For example, according
to this convention, the tile T1 still has just four vertices, but the tile T4 has
five vertices (because we convene that the point denoted Q124 is a vertex of
T4 ). We also extend this abuse of terminology to edges, and we say that the
impose that the image of each face via ΨP  3 is exactly the corresponding tile. Nevertheless,
we can impose that this image approximates the corresponding tile as accurately as we
want, and this will be sufficient for our goals.


                                             34
tile T4 has five edges. (This unusual terminology will become very convenient
soon, because it will allow us to say that each face Fi of the polyhedral surface
P(B(F2P )) has the same number of vertices and the same number of edges as
its corresponding tile Ti .)

Remark. Ideally, if it was possible, we would have liked to simply construct
polygonal faces Fi of the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P )) such that

                                      ΨP3 (Fi ) = Ti ,

i.e., such that the “logarithmic projective image” of each face Fi is the tile
Ti . Unfortunately, it turns out that this is impossible in 3D (although it was
possible in 2D). Instead, we will make sure that the logarithmic projective
image of each face Fi is a very good approximation of the tile Ti , i.e.,

                                      ΨP3 (Fi ) ≈ Ti ,

in a sense that will be clarified below. In particular, the vertices and edges
of Fi will be in a “canonical” one-to-one correspondence with vertices and
edges51 of Ti , and the images via ΨP3 of vertices and edges of Fi can be made
to lie arbitrarily closely to the corresponding vertices and edges of Ti .

    We now start with the tile T1 , and explain how we construct the face F1 .
We see that T1 has just four edges, so F1 will also have four edges. First
we build an edge of F1 that corresponds to the left-side edge of T1 , denoted
[Q0 Q14 ] in Figure 5(a). For this, we first choose a point P0 of coordinates
(ε, ε, ε), for some positive number ε ≪ 1. Note that for any positive ε we
have
                                ΨP3 (P0 ) = Q0 .
Then we draw a line segment that lies within the plane {x2 = x3 }, is orthog-
onal to the point (1, 1, 1), and advances inside the set {x1 ≥ x2 = x3 } (see
Figure 5(b))52 . We extend this line segment within the set {x1 ≥ x2 = x3 }

line that starts at P12 , goes into the set {x1 ≥ x2 ≥ x3 }, and is orthogonal to
the basepoints of T1 and T2 ; and also construct a half-line that starts at P14 ,
goes into the set {x1 ≥ x2 ≥ x3 }, and is orthogonal to the basepoints of T1
and T4 ; and now define P124 as the intersection point of these two half-lines.
    Note that, if such an intersection point exists, then we have successfully
obtained the complete face F1 , and this face F1 is guaranteed to be orthogonal
to the basepoint of T1 , because all its edges are orthogonal to the basepoint
of T1 .
    Let us show now that this intersection point P124 does indeed exist. (A
priori, even though we know that these two half-lines lie in the same plane54 ,
this is not sufficient to immediately conclude that they must have a common
point.) One way to see this is to use the following two things:

     Note that once we have decided that each face Fi must be orthogonal to the basepoint

construction is “canonical”, once we have chosen a value of ε. Even if we don’t consider

                                               38
following:
    (i) The construction of points and edges along the boundary (i.e., within

    (ii) If an edge eij is adjacent to the faces Fi and Fj then eij must be
orthogonal to the basepoints of the tiles Ti and Tj .
    (iii) If a vertex Pi of a face Fi corresponds to a “degenerate” vertex Qi
of the tile Ti , then the X3P -coordinate of ΨP3 (Pi ) must match exactly the
X3P -coordinate of the point Qi .

that we construct, and is obtained by applying the rule (ii) simultaneously
to construct the two edges that meet at Pi .
    Note that for edges that correspond to the top side or the left side of the
blue box we have to impose that they are orthogonal to the basepoint of one
of the two “boundary tiles”, and this basepoint lies at infinity. Nevertheless,
the orthogonality condition males sense in these cases as well. (If a line
segment ℓ is orthogonal to a “regular” basepoint Bi and also is orthogonal to
the basepoint Bj that lies at infinity, then it means that ℓ is orthogonal to
Bi and to the line in the X2 -X3 -plane whose slope is given by the point Bj ).
    Finally, we now discuss the construction of the two faces that correspond
to the two “boundary tiles”, denoted T10 and T11 .

D2 (instead of D2P ), see Figure 7. In general, it is more convenient to use
   H

D2P for tiles that lie inside the blue box (because we can take advantage of the
simplicity of horizontal and vertical lines within D2P , while within D2H the
same lines are not actually parallel; instead, they meet at some boundary
point59 ). On the other hand, it can be better to use D2H for tiles that lie
outside the blue box; for example, the use of D2H for these “tiles near infinity”
comes with the advantage that their basepoints have a simple “finite” location
in D2H (while their basepoints lie at infinity in D2P ).

6.1.3    The polyhedral surface P(B(F2P )) gives rise to a ZSH
We now explain why the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P )) can be used for the
construction of a ZSH for any initial condition x0 (for well-chosen ε).

  Let us first explain why, if ε0 is small enough, then the polyhedral surface
P(B(F2P )) satisfies the ZSH property within the unit cube (0, 1)3 .
  58
     We assume that we have already constructed the edge of F10 that lies within the plane

          We start by noticing some simple geometric correspondences between the
      relative locations of vertices, edges, faces of the subdivision F2P , and the tiles
      of B(F2P ), and also the images of faces60 of the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P ))
      via the map ΨP3 , see Figure 4(b) and Figure 5(e):
      1. For any vertex v of the subdivision F2P there exists a tile Ti of B(F2P )
      which has v as its basepoint. Moreover, the face Fi of P(B(F2P )) has the
      property that ΨP3 (Fi ) is a neighborhood of the vertex v within the set D2P .
      2. For any edge e of the subdivision F2P there exists two tiles Ti , Tj of B(F2P )
      which have the endpoints of e as their basepoints. Moreover, the faces Fi , Fj
      of P(B(F2P )) have the property that ΨP3 (Fi ∪ Fj ) is a neighborhood of the
      edge e within the set D2P .
      3. For any face f of the subdivision F2P consider the tiles Ti1 , Ti2 , ..., Tik of
      B(F2P ) which have the property61 that their basepoints belong to f . More-
      over, the faces Fi1 , Fi2 , ..., Fik of P(B(F2P )) have the property that ΨP3 (Fi1 ∪
      Fi2 ∪ ... ∪ Fik ) is a neighborhood of the face f within the set D2P .
        60
            The observations 1-3 about images of faces of P(B(F2P )) take advantage of the as-
      sumption that ε0 is small enough. Indeed, for small enough ε0 the set ΨP  3 (Fi ) is arbitrarily
      close to the tile Ti , so it is enough to check that “Ti is a neighborhood of v”, or “Ti ∪ Tj
      is a neighborhood of e”, and so on.
         61
            It is easy to see in Figure 4(b) that we have either k = 3 or k = 4. The case k = 3
      corresponds to a face f that has a vertex or an edge at infinity, and the case k = 4
      corresponds to a face f that is contained in the blue box.


                                                           41
    This means that we can now apply Lemma 9.7 (for cones KC that are de-
fined using the neighborhoods we pointed out above62 ) and conclude that, for
ε0 small enough, the toric differential inclusion T3 cannot cross the polyhedral
surface P(B(F2P )) within the set (0, 1)3 .

    For a fixed x0 ∈ R3>0 we first fix a specific level surface L of the Horn-
Jackson Lyapunov function such that x0 is below that level surface (see
Lemma 9.11 for details on the shape of these level surfaces). Let us also
fix some M > 1 such that the whole surface L lies inside the cube [0, M ]3 .
    We claim that, if we choose ε0 small enough63 then we can ensure that the
toric differential inclusion T3 cannot cross the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P ))
anywhere within the cube64 [0, M ]3 .
    We already know that the toric differential inclusion T3 cannot cross the
polyhedral surface P(B(F2P )) within the cube [0, 1]3 . Let us also recall that
we have constructed P(B(F2P )) in the set {0 < x3 ≤ x2 ≤ x1 } by starting
with a polygonal surface S0 that was contained within a neighborhood of
the origin of size O(ε0 ) and then by building cylindrical surfaces along the
boundary of S0 .
    Consider now a point P ∈ P(B(F2P )) ∩ [0, M ]3 within the set {0 < x3 ≤
x2 ≤ x1 }, and outside the unit cube [0, 1]3 . We will argue that the toric
differential inclusion T3 cannot cross the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P )) at P .
    The point P = (x̃1 , x̃2 , x̃3 ) was obtained from S0 by the cylindrical con-
struction mentioned above. Therefore, at least one coordinate of P must be
very small; more precisely, we must have x̃3 = O(ε0 ). On the other hand, we
  62
      The fact that Ψ3 (Fi ) approximates Ti very closely (see Figure 5(e)) implies the fol-

or a face in the subdivision F2P , and our claim is easy to check for each one of these cases,

   63
      Recall that ε0 was a very small positive number which we chose when we positioned

   64
      Initially we have focused on the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P )) within the unit cube

all the way to infinity), because there is no problem to extend the cylindrical faces of
P(B(F2P )) outside [0, 1]3 . We need this larger version of P(B(F2P )) because later we will
intersect it with the level surface L of the Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function.

also must have
                               0 < log(x̃1 ) < log(M ),

                                   log(x̃1 )
                                                         ∈ (−η, 0),
                       log(x̃1 ) + log(x̃2 ) + log(x̃3 )

    Therefore, if ε0 is small enough, the ray along the vector log(P ) is very
close to the cones of F3 that lie along the boundary of D2H where X1H = 0,
denoted ∂1 D2H .
    Note now that every cone C of F3 that lies close enough to ∂1 D2H must intersect65
∂1 D2H , and therefore, if ε0 is small enough, the right-hand side of the toric
differential inclusion T3 at P will not depend on C, but on the intersection66
between C and ∂1 D2H . But C ∩ ∂1 D2H is one of the points or line segments ly-
ing along ∂1 D2H , which we have already considered in our construction of the
surface P(B(F2P )). In conclusion, the toric differential inclusion T3 cannot
cross the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P )) at P .

   In the next section we will consider the case of a fully general fan F3 ,
and we will see that the construction of the ZSH blueprint within the blue
box can become more complicated, and also that we will need to allow for
any finite number of “tiles near infinity” (as opposed to just two such tiles in
the special case of the fan F3 we used in this section). Nevertheless, a very
similar approach will allow us to construct a ZSH in the general case.


6.2     The general construction of ZSH in 3D
In the previous section we have discussed the construction of ZSH in 3D for a
convenient choice of polyhedral fan F3 (and corresponding subdivisions F2P
and F2H ). We now consider the general case for F3 .
    Recall that F3 gives rise to two versions of F2 , one (denoted F2P ) within
D2P and another (denoted F2H ) within D2H . (Like before, without loss of
generality, we assume that F3 is X1 -X2 -X3 -symmetric, and this ensures that
  65
      Because any cone that does not intersect ∂1 D2H must lie at some positive distance
from ∂1 D2H , and there are finitely many cones in F3 .
   66
      Because the right-hand side of a toric differential inclusion T at a point P depends
only on the smallest cone of the fan of T that is close enough to the point log P .


                                           43
      all relevant information about F3 is contained in F2P , and also in F2H .) Note
      also that the information contained in F2P is equivalent to the information
      contained in F2H .
          Our strategy for the construction of ZSH will rely again on a finite par-
      tition of D2P (and, equivalently D2H ) using well-chosen quadrilateral “tiles”
      (most of these tiles will be rectangular, with the exception of tiles lying along
      the boundary of D2P ). Like in the previous section, our plan is to construct a
      ZSH that has exactly one face for each “tile”; we will refer to this partition
      into tiles as a “ZSH blueprint”. Once we have built a ZSH blueprint we will
      see that the construction of the ZSH can proceed in the same way as in the
      previous section.

      Consider a given F2P in D2P , as shown in Figure 8(a). We can see that the
      F2P in Figure 8(a) is much more complicated than the one we have shown
      in Figure 4(a). In particular, we see that the affine half-lines present in F2P
      have four different slopes, as opposed to just 2 different slopes (zero & one)
      in Figure 4(a). More importantly, in Figure 4 we have avoided triangular
      regions in F2P , while in Figure 8 there are many triangular regions in F2P .

      type of blueprint we constructed in the previous section for this F2P . Never-
      theless, we can construct a blueprint for this F2P by proceeding step by step
      as illustrated in Figure 9.

    The key idea for the construction of the ZSH blueprint shown in Fig-

stages: first choose a small enough67 height for the blue horizontal strips that
cover the horizontal half-lines of F2P , and partition them into quadrilater-

smaller68 height for the orange horizontal strips, in order to be able to parti-

intersecting exactly one one-dimensional element of F2P . Also, we choose
the basepoints of these orange quadrilaterals to lie on this one-dimensional
element of F2P , at a height that is exactly along the midline of each horizon-
tal orange strip, as shown in Figure 9(g). (A fully general discussion of the
existence of such a blueprint for any fan F3 in R3>0 , and also for any fan Fn
in Rn>0 will be given in Section 7.)
