6.2.2     The use the ZSH blueprint in the construction of the ZSH
In general, once we have a ZSH blueprint as described in Figure 9 and Fig-
ure 10, the construction of the polyhedral ZSH is analogous to the construction
described in the previous section.
    For faces of the ZSH that correspond to tiles that lie inside the blue box
the construction is completely similar. (Note that, like in the previous sec-
tion, we have ensured that pairs of tiles that are adjacent horizontally satisfy
the important property that their basepoints lie on the same horizontal line.
This implies that any nonzero vector v = (v1 , v2 , v3 ) that is orthogonal to two
such basepoints must have v3 = 0. This allows us to apply Lemma 9.10(ii) to
conclude that for any edge e shared by such a pair of tiles its corresponding
edge ê within the ZSH satisfies the property that ΨP3 (ê) will be arbitrarily
close71 to e if ε0 is small enough.)
    For faces of the ZSH that correspond to tiles that lie outside the blue box
the construction is also similar (i.e., we just build the cylindrical surface that
starts along the outer edges of the blue box (when seen in D2P ) and uses the
direction of the x1 -axis as its generator). On the other hand, the setting in
Section 3 was simpler, with only two such “boundary tiles”, so we will look
again at the representation of F3 in D2H (beside its representation in D2P ) in
order to understand precisely these boundary faces.
  69
     Recall from the previous section that images via ΨP    3 of lines that are parallel to the x1 -
axis are lines that pass through the origin. Therefore, this particular choice for the three
unbounded dotted blue lines will be compatible later with our construction of the ZSH
faces that correspond to boundary tiles as part of a cylindrical surface whose generating
direction is the direction of the x1 -axis.
  70
     The reason we have four tiles in Figure 10(a) is that there are four different such slopes
for half-lines of F2P .
  71
     The most important information that we derive from Lemma 9.10(ii) is that the
tangent direction to any point of ΨP  3 (ê) is very close to vertical.




                                                47
    When we look at the four boundary tiles in D2H we can see that each one
has a well defined basepoint (which specifies the normal of the corresponding
face of the ZSH) and that these basepoints lie on the plane {X1 = 0}, which
confirms the fact that each one of these four “outer faces” are supported by
planes that are parallel to the x1 -axis.
    The fact that the polyhedral surface P(B(F2P )) discussed in this section is
indeed a ZSH (and that T3 cannot cross this ZSH within any cube [0, M ]3 if we
choose ε small enough) can be argued exactly like in the previous section72 .




  72
     Some of the key observations 1-3 about images of faces of P(B(F2P )) need to be
modified slightly. For example, in observation “2.” for some edges e of the subdivision
F2P there are more than two tiles whose basepoints lie on e (and these basepoints are not
necessarily endpoints of e), so we need to use a union of faces that correspond to these
tiles, but this does not change anything relevant in the proof. Also, in observation “3.”
it is no longer true that any face f of F2P can be covered with just three or four tiles of
B(F2P ), but this also does not change anything relevant in the proof.


                                            48
7      Subdivisions in Rn, their ZSH pre-blueprints,
       and their faithful ZSH blueprints
We have already seen that key properties of 3D toric differential inclusion
T3 can be represented by a 2D subdivision F2P that is obtained from the 3D
polyhedral fan F3 of T3 . Also, we have seen how a 2D ZSH blueprint B(F2P )
can be used for constructing a ZSH in 3D.
    Here we will extend this approach to nD, while also modifying the 2D
construction accordingly, in order to be able to include it in the framework
of an induction on dimension.
    For example, the general 2D subdivisions that we consider here are no
longer restricted to the subset D2P ⊂ R2 , see Figure 11(a); similarly, in this
section nD subdivisions will be defined on the whole Rn , instead of being
restricted to a subset of it.
    Moreover, instead of just ZSH blueprints, we will also discuss ZSH pre-
blueprints, and use them as a key tool for constructing faithful ZSH blueprints,
which will play an especially important role here. Also, in this section these
pre-blueprints and blueprints will be defined on the whole Euclidean space
(i.e., they will not be restricted to a subset of it, as in Section 6).
    See Figure 11(b) for an example of a ZSH pre-blueprint, and see Fig-
ure 14(g) for an illustration of a faithful ZSH blueprint.

7.1     Polyhedral fans and subdivisions in Rn
Recall that by a “fan” we mean a complete and pointed polyhedral fan. We
start by defining a special kind of fan, called x1 -xn -fan. The definition pro-
ceeds inductively, for all n ≥ 2, as follows.
     An x1 -x2 -fan F2 is a fan in R2 that contains both of the 1D cones (i.e.,
rays) that lie along the x2 -axis.
     An x1 -x3 -fan F3 is a fan in R3 such that there exists a x1 -x2 -fan F2 in
  2
R with the property that π3 (F3 ) = F2 , where π3 is the standard projection
from R3 to R2 . This means that, in particular, the half-planes in R3 that
project to rays of F2 must be unions of cones of F3 . Also, the set π3−1 ({0}),
i.e., the x3 -axis, must be a union of cones of F3 , namely the positive ray and
the negative ray of the x3 -axis73 .
  73
    Note that we could have also defined an “x1 -x1 -fan” to be any fan in R1 , and then
an equivalent definition of an x1 -x2 -fan could have been a fan F2 in R2 such that there


                                           49
           (a)




           (b)


Figure 11: In (a) we see an example of an x1 -x2 -subdivision S2 , and in (b) we see a ZSH pre-blueprint
for it.



Similarly, in general, a x1 -xn -fan Fn is a fan in Rn such that there exists a
x1 -xn−1 -fan Fn−1 in Rn−1 with the property that πn (Fn ) = Fn−1 .

   We will now define some polyhedral subdivisions of Rn called x1 -xn -
subdivisions, which are strongly related to x1 -xn -fans. Consider the embed-
exists a x1 -x1 -fan F1 in R1 such that π2 (F2 ) = F1 , i.e., would have been analogous to the
definition of an x1 -x3 -fan. (By the way, note also that there exists actually only one fan
in R1 , because we only consider complete fans.)


                                                  50
ding
                                 in : Rn → Rn+1
obtained by mapping Rn to the hyperplane {x1 = 1} in Rn+1 via

                        in (x1 , ..., xn ) = (1, x1 , ..., xn ).

Then an x1 -xn -subdivision Sn is a polyhedral subdivision of Rn that can
be obtained by using the embedding in to identify Rn with the hyperplane
{x1 = 1} of Rn+1 , and then taking the intersection of this hyperplane with
all the cones of a x1 -xn+1 -fan Fn+1 . In other words, up to the identification
given by in , we have

                      Sn = {C ∩ {x1 = 1} | C ∈ Fn+1 }.

In particular, note that this implies that for any x1 -xn -subdivision Sn there
exists an x1 -xn−1 -subdivision Sn−1 such that πn (Sn ) = Sn−1 .
    An element of an x1 -xn -subdivision Sn is called a face of Sn , i.e., up to
the identification given by in , a face of Sn is a nonempty intersection between
some cone C ∈ Fn+1 and the plane {x1 = 1}.
    In subsection 7.3 will define ZSH pre-blueprints for any x1 -xn -subdivision
Sn , and in subsection 7.4 we will use ZSH pre-blueprints in order to define
faithful ZSH blueprints for any x1 -xn -subdivision Sn .

7.2    Binary words for faces of an x1 -xn -subdivision Sn
Consider an x1 -xn -subdivision Sn . First, note that to any face ∆0 ∈ Sn we
can associate a binary word of length n denoted

                         α(∆0 ) = α1 a2 ...an ∈ {0, 1}n ,

as follows. Consider the face πn (∆0 ) in Rn−1 ; if we have

                           dim(πn (∆0 )) = dim(∆0 )

then we define αn = 0, and if

                         dim(πn (∆0 )) = dim(∆0 ) − 1

then we define αn = 1. Similarly, we define

                 αn−1 = dim(πn (∆0 )) − dim(πn−1 (πn (∆0 ))),

                                          51
and so on. In other words, as we consider the successive projections πn , πn−1 ,
πn−2 , ..., π1 of ∆0 , the binary letter αj tells us if the j th projection πj did or
did not cause its dimension to decrease by one unit. Equivalently, but in the
opposite order, we can think about ∆0 as having been “grown” by starting
from a single point 0 ∈ R0 , and then its dimension went up by one unit at
every stage j that has αj = 1.


7.3     ZSH pre-blueprints of an x1 -xn -subdivision Sn
In this subsection we introduce and study the notion of ZSH pre-blueprint
associated to an x1 -xn -subdivision Sn . Our main goal in this section is to
show that we can construct ZSH blueprints for Sn , and the construction of
ZSH pre-blueprints in this subsection will be the most important step towards
that goal.

    We first define one-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprints; these are sets of in-
tervals with disjoint interiors that cover R1 and have a strong relationship
with a given x1 -x1 -subdivision. Consider an x1 -x1 -subdivision S1 , as shown
in Figure 12. In general, S1 consists of a finite set of points (i.e., 0-faces)
and a finite set of closed intervals (i.e., 1-faces) whose endpoints are those
0-faces.




            Figure 12: An example of an x1 -x1 -subdivision S1 of R1 .


   A ZSH pre-blueprint of S1 is given by an assignment of a closed interval
denoted nbhd (σ) for any σ ∈ S1 such that there exists some positive number
denoted ε(0) for which we have
                          nbhd (σ0 ) = σ0 + [−ε(0), ε(0)]
for any 0-face σ0 ∈ S1 , and
                                               [
                         nbhd (σ1 ) = σ1 \             nbhd (σ0 )
                                              σ0 ∈S1


                                         52
for any 1-face σ1 ∈ S1 (where the union above is over 0-faces σ0 ∈ S1 ).
Moreover, we require that ε(0) is small enough so the interiors of the intervals
nbhd (σ) are disjoint for all σ ∈ S1 .
    More precisely, in general, a ZSH pre-blueprint pB1 of S1 as described
above is defined as the set of intervals nbhd (σ), i.e., we have
                            p
                             B1 = {nbhd (σ) | σ ∈ S1 }.

Informally, we can think of “nbhd ” as a function that associates a subset of
R to any σ ∈ S1 , according to the rules described above. Note then that
the function nbhd uniquely determines the set pB1 ; also, less obviously, the
set of intervals pB1 uniquely determines the function nbhd . Indeed, given
the set pB1 and some zero-dimensional σ0 ∈ S1 , we can define nbhd (σ0 )
to be the (unique) element of pB1 that contains the point σ0 ; and for any
one-dimensional σ1 ∈ S1 , we can define nbhd (σ1 ) to be the (again, unique)
element of pB1 that intersects σ1 and was not already assigned to be the
nbhd (σ0 ) for some zero-dimensional σ0 ∈ S1 .

    We will now define two-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprints, i.e., ZSH pre-
blueprints associated to x1 -x2 -subdivisions; these are composed of some spe-
cial polygonal sets with disjoint interiors, which cover R2 and have a strong
relationship with a given x1 -x2 -subdivision.
    Consider an x1 -x2 -subdivision S2 that projects to an x1 -x1 -subdivision
denoted S1 . We define a ZSH pre-blueprint pB2 of S2 as follows. First, we
assume that we have already constructed a ZSH pre-blueprint pB1 of S1 , for
some ε(0) > 0 (on which additional restrictions will be imposed below).
Note now that there are four types of faces in S2 , corresponding to the
binary words 00, 01, 10, 11. Specifically, zero-dimensional faces σ00 ∈ S2
have α(σ00 ) = 00 and are just points in R2 ; one-dimensional faces σ01 ∈ S2
with α(σ01 ) = 01 are edges that are parallel to the x2 -axis; one-dimensional
faces σ10 ∈ S2 with α(σ10 ) = 10 are edges that are not parallel to the x2 -axis;
and, finally, two-dimensional faces σ11 ∈ S2 with α(σ11 ) = 11 are polygons74 .
Consider some positive numbers ε(00) and ε(10) and define ε(01) = ε(0).
Informally, it will be convenient to assume that we have

                         0 < ε(10) ≪ ε(01) ≪ ε(00) ≪ 1;

this will be made more precise below.
 74
      Some edges and some polygons are unbounded.


                                         53
As in the one-dimensional case, we will now define a set nbhd (σ) for any
σ ∈ S2 . Consider first a zero-dimensional face σ00 ∈ S2 . We define

              nbhd (σ00 ) = σ00 + [−ε(01), ε(01)] × [−ε(00), ε(00)].

If σ10 ∈ S2 has α(σ10 ) = 10 then we define

          nbhd (σ10 ) = (σ10 + [−ε(10), ε(10)]) ∩ (nbhd (π2 (σ10 )) × R) .

For the faces of the form σ01 and σ11 (i.e., having corresponding binary words
01 and 11, respectively) we define their nbhd by taking advantage of the ones
already defined above. Specifically, for an edge σ01 ∈ S2 we define nbhd (σ01 )
to be the subset of

that is delimited by nbhd (σ00      ) and nbhd (σ00   ), where σ00 and σ00 are the
endpoints of σ01 . (If σ01 is unbounded then only one such delimiter is needed.)

                           ′          ′′                                    ′

are disjoint for all σ ′ ̸= σ ′′ ∈ S2 . It is easy to see in 2D that (for a fixed

Finally, this allows us to conclude that the construction above gives rise to

    Assume now that we have defined ZSH pre-blueprints for x1 -xn−1 -subdivisons;
we will now define ZSH pre-blueprints of an x1 -xn -subdivison Sn .
First, we consider some real-valued function ε̂(α) whose domain is the set of
all binary words of length k ≤ n, such that the function ε̂ satisfies

                                      ε̂(α1 α2 ...αk−1 0) > 0

and also
                                     ε̂(α1 α2 ...αk−1 1) = 0.
Then we define the fiber of a binary word α = α1 α2 ...αn to be

       fiber (α) = [−ε̂(α̂1 ), ε̂(α̂1 )] × [−ε̂(α̂2 ), ε̂(α̂2 )] × ... × [−ε̂(α̂n ), ε̂(α̂n )],

where α̂j denotes the prefix of α of length j, i.e., α̂j = α1 α2 ...αj .
Then, if σ ∈ Sn has binary type α = α1 α2 ...αn−1 0, we define

                    nbhd (σ) = (σ + fiber (α)) ∩ nbhd (πn (σ)) × R.

On the other hand, if α = α1 α2 ...αn−1 1, then we define nbhd (σ) to be the
closed subset of
                           nbhd (πn (σ)) × R
that is delimited by78 nbhd (σ ′ ) and nbhd (σ ′′ ), where σ ′ and σ ′′ are the facets79
of σ that satisfy
                          πn (σ ′ ) = πn (σ ′′ ) = πn (σ).
  77
      Because, even if the edge σ of binary type 10 has very small slope (in absolute value),

                                                 55
(Like we saw before, some unbounded σ may only have one such facet σ ′ . If

one side by nbhd (σ ′ ).) Moreover, we impose that the interiors of nbhd (σ ′ )
and nbhd (σ ′′ ) are disjoint for all σ ′ ̸= σ ′′ ∈ Sn .

    Of course, it is not obvious that the construction of n-dimensional ZSH
pre-blueprints described above is always possible. The theorem below tells
us that for well-chosen values of ε̂(α) we can guarantee that this construction
is possible.
    In order to formulate this theorem, recall that we have discussed above
the real-valued function ε̂(α); based on such a function we define another
real-valued function ε(α), which is only defined for binary words α of length
exactly n, and is given by

                          ε(α1 α2 ...αn−1 0) = ε̂(α1 α2 ...αn−1 0)

and
                      ε(α1 α2 ...αk−1 011...1) = ε̂(α1 α2 ...αk−1 0).
In other words, the value of ε(α) is the same as the value of ε̂(α̂), where α̂
is obtained from α by erasing all the “1” bits at the end of α. Note that, in
particular, we have ε(α) > 0 for all80 binary words α of length n.

Theorem 7.1. Consider an x1 -xn -subdivison Sn and some functions ε̂(α)
and ε(α) as described above. If the number
                     n            ε(00...01) ε(00...10)        ε(11...10) o
       ε(pBn ) := max ε(00...00),           ,           , ...,                          (12)
                                  ε(00...00) ε(00...01)        ε(11...01)

is small enough81 , then the construction of a ZSH pre-blueprint pBn of Sn
described above is well defined. In particular, if σ ′ ̸= σ ′′ ∈ Sn , then the
interiors of nbhd (σ ′ ) and nbhd (σ ′′ ) are disjoint.

Proof. We proceed by induction, so we assume that we already know this to
be true in dimensions ≤ n − 1.

  81
     Note that this is essentially equivalent to saying that we have ε(11...10) ≪ ε(11...01) ≪
... ≪ ε(00...10) ≪ ε(00...01) ≪ ε(00...00) ≪ 1, and therefore the magnitude sizes of the
numbers ε(α) grow exactly in the opposite direction than the standard ordering of the
binary numbers given by the binary words α.

for the projections of Sn in dimensions 1, 2, ..., n − 1.
Then, if the quantity in (12) is small enough, we can apply the induction

of pBn , and it follows that the interiors of nbhd (πn (σ ′ )) and nbhd (πn (σ ′′ ))
are disjoint for all σ ′ , σ ′′ ∈ Sn such that πn (σ ′ ) ̸= πn (σ ′′ ), and therefore the
interiors of nbhd (σ ′ ) and nbhd (σ ′′ ) are also disjoint for all σ ′ , σ ′′ ∈ Sn such

     Therefore, it is now sufficient to show that nbhd (σ ′ ) and nbhd (σ ′′ ) are
disjoint for those σ ′ , σ ′′ ∈ Sn such that πn (σ ′ ) = πn (σ ′′ ). Moreover, it is
sufficient to consider the case where σ ′ and σ ′′ have binary type α of the
form α1 α2 ...αn−1 082 ; in particular, we then have dim(σ ′ ) = dim(σ ′′ ).
     If dim(σ ′ ) ≤ n − 2, then σ ′ and σ ′′ lie in a common linear subspace of
dimension ≤ n − 1, and we can use the induction hypothesis to conclude that
nbhd (σ ′ ) and nbhd (σ ′′ ) are disjoint. (Alternatively, we could use the same
argument as presented below for the case dim(σ ′ ) = n − 1, but formulate it
in a subspace of dimension equal to dim(σ ′ ) + 1.)
     If dim(σ ′ ) = n − 1, then σ ′ and σ ′′ have binary type 11...110. In this case,
it is sufficient to consider the case where dim(σ ′ ∩ σ ′′ ) is as large as possible83 ,
i.e., dim(σ ′ ∩ σ ′′ ) = n − 2.

be checked directly in dimensions 1 or 2, and if we assume it to be true in
dimension n − 1, then we notice that in dimension n we only have to check
it for faces σ that satisfy dim πn (σ) = n − 1, since for all other σ ∈ Sn the
desired result follows from the induction hypothesis (this is similar to our
use of induction hypothesis in the proof of Theorem 7.1).
    Now choose σ that satisfies dim πn (σ) = n − 1 and consider first the case
where σ has binary type of the form 11...10. If we choose some point P ∈ σ,

                                              60
7.4     From ZSH pre-blueprints to faithful ZSH blueprints
In the previous section we have discussed the construction of ZSH pre-
blueprints of an x1 -xn -subdivision Sn for any n. On the other hand, our
ultimate goal is actually construction of ZSH, which requires a ZSH blueprint
of Sn . Here we discuss how we can use ZSH pre-blueprints in order to con-
struct associated faithful ZSH blueprints, and why these are useful.
    A faithful ZSH blueprint Bnff of Sn is a special kind of ZSH blueprint,
which is strongly related to a given pre-blueprint pBn of Sn . In particular, for
each σ ∈ Sn , if we denote by f -nbhd (σ) the union of all the tiles Tn of Bnff
such that the basepoint of Tn belongs to σ, then f -nbhd (σ) can approximate
the set nbhd (σ) of pBn arbitrarily well, in a sense that will be clarified below
(see Figure 14 for an illustration).
    More importantly, an n-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint can be used
for the construction of an (n+1)-dimensional ZSH blueprint. Moreover, given
enough additional information86 (in a sense that will be discussed below), an
n-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint can be used for the construction of an
(n + 1)-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint. Therefore, we will see that the
use of faithful ZSH blueprints will allow us to construct ZSH blueprints in
any dimension.

7.4.1    The one-dimensional case
We define a one-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint of a one-dimensional
x1 -x1 -subdivision S1 as being obtained from a one-dimensional ZSH pre-
blueprint87 pB1 of S1 as follows. We assume that we already are given an
x1 -x2 -subdivision S2 such that S1 = π2 (S2 ), and a two-dimensional ZSH pre-
blueprint pB2 of S2 such that pB1 = π2 (pB2 )88 . Let us fix a number denoted
  86
     We will see that this additional information will come from properties of an (n + 2)-
dimensional ZSH pre-blueprint. This is not a problem, because we already know how to
construct ZSH pre-blueprints in any dimension.
  87
     Note that a one-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprint is actually also a one-dimensional ZSH
blueprint.
  88
     It is important to note that, by definition, we cannot just look at a one-dimensional
ZSH blueprint of S1 in isolation and say whether it is “faithful” or not. The property of
being “faithful” depends on relationships between this one-dimensional ZSH blueprint of
S1 and some two-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprint of S2 .

For each σ ∈ S1 such that ε(σ) = 1 we divide the interval nbhd (σ) into very

7.4.2     The two-dimensional case
Some of the main ideas on how to construct a faithful ZSH blueprint in the
two-dimensional case are illustrated in Figure 14.
    Note that the sets nbhd (σ) are already rectangular if α(σ) = 00 or α(σ) =
10, see Figure 11(b).
    Our goal is to “modify” the ZSH pre-blueprint in such a way that nbhd (σ)
is approximated by a set of rectangles for the cases where α(σ) = 10 or
α(σ) = 11.
    We can see in Figure 14(b) that it is easy to place a “tower of offset
rectangles” such that they approximate the region of nbhd (σ) in the case
where α(σ) = 10. The most convenient way to do this is to use rectangles that
have the same type of aspect ratio as the blue rectangles that we have already
used in the ZSH pre-blueprint, when we built nbhd (σ) for zero-dimensional
σ, i.e., with α(σ) = 00, see the red rectangles in Figure 11(b).
    Here is why using red rectangles with this particular type aspect ratio
(i.e., “thin and long” rectangles) is useful: recall that we constructed the
blue rectangles in Figure 11(b) such that their width is much larger that their
height91 . Then this type of “thin and long” rectangle spans across92 the edge
   89
      Note that ε̃(1) depends on ε(10), and the information about ε(10) comes from pB2 .

mean that, once we are given the S2 and pB2 , then there exists some ε̃0 ∈ (0, ε(10)) which
depends only on S2 and pB2 , such that if we have ε̃(1) < ε̃0 , then we say that we have
ε̃(1) ≪ ε(10).
   90
      Since we have ε̃(1) ≪ 1, and the length of any interval nbhd (σ) considered above is

Note that we cannot guarantee their size to be exactly ε̃(1), because we don’t know that
this number is an integer factor of the length of nbhd (σ).

   92

σ if we place its centerpoint93 on the edge σ.

     We would like to think about the construction of a two-dimensional faith-
ful ZSH blueprint B2ff for S2 as part of an inductive process, i.e., a preparation
for the later construction of an n-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint Bnff for
Sn .

Step 1. Before we construct B2ff let us discuss how we can construct just an
ordinary (not “faithful”) ZSH blueprint B2 . Then, in Step 2, we will further
refine this construction to obtain B2ff .
    In order to construct B2 we will rely on the following three pieces of
information: (i) a one-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprint pB1 of S1 = π2 (S2 ),
(ii) a two-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprint pB2 of S2 such that pB1 = π2 (pB2 ),
and (iii) a one-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint B2ff of S1 94 .
    For each vertex σ0 ∈ S2 (i.e., zero-dimensional face95 of S2 ) we define
the tile of σ0 to be precisely nbhd (σ0 ), and we define its basepoint to be the
vertex σ0 .
    For each edge σ1 ∈ S2 of binary type α(σ1 ) = 01 (i.e., horizontal edge in
Figure 14(a)) similarly we define the tile of σ1 to be precisely nbhd (σ1 ), and
we define its basepoint to be its centerpoint.
    For any edge σ ∈ S2 of binary type α(σ) = 10, we define rectangular
tiles along σ as illustrated by the red rectangles in Figure 14(e), i.e., such
that each such tile T2 projects via π2 to a tile T1 of π2 (S2 ) that covers a part
of nbhd (π2 (σ)). Also, we choose the basepoint of each such tile T2 to be its
centerpoint, and to lie on σ. Note that for each such tile T2 its height is
determined by the size of T1 , so we only have to specify its width; we choose
its width to be ε(10)96 .
blueprint B2ff that we are constructing.

                                             64
   Finally, for any face σ2 ∈ S2 of binary type α(σ) = 11, note that σ2 has
two97 edges σ ′ and σ ′′ such that

                               π2 (σ2 ) = π2 (σ ′ ) = π2 (σ ′′ ),

and the set nbhd (σ2 ) is delimited within the set

                                    nbhd (π2 (σ2 )) × R

by nbhd (σ ′ ) and nbhd (σ ′′ ).
    Moreover, the edges σ ′ and σ ′′ have binary type 10, so we have already
constructed the tiles that are associated to them (i.e., the tiles that have
basepoints on them). For each tile T1 of π2 (S2 ) that has basepoint on π2 (σ)
there exist two tiles T2′ and T2′′ that have basepoints on σ ′ and σ ′′ (as suggested
in Figure 14(e)) and we use them as delimiters within the set

                                           T1 × R,

in order to define the tiles associated to σ2 to be the rectangles delimited as
we discussed above (i.e., the thin black rectangles in Figure 14(e)).

Step 2. Let us now discuss the construction of the two-dimensional faithful
ZSH blueprint B2ff . This construction will be a refinement of the construc-
tion of B2 , and will rely on additional information that comes from a three-
dimensional x1 -x3 -subdivision S3 , and a ZSH pre-blueprint pB3 of S3 , such
that we have π3 (S3 ) = S2 and π3 (pB3 ) = pB2 98 .
     Recall that when we constructed the one-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint
  ff
B1 we made the decision to further subdivide nbhd (σ1 ) for any edge σ1 of S1 ;
for this we needed to decide how small will the new tiles be within nbhd (σ1 ),
and we decided to impose the condition that the new tiles will have length
approximately ε̃(1), such that

                                       ε̃(1) ≪ ε(10).
  97
      If σ2 is unbounded then there is just one such edge, say σ ′ , and nbhd (σ) is delimited
by nbhd (σ ′ ).
   98
      Recall that, in the earlier construction of the one-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint

                                              65
Recall also the reason behind this decision was that we wanted to make sure
that if we were to use one-dimensional tiles of (approximate) size ε̃(1) in a π2 -
compatible two-dimensional construction, then the resulting two-dimensional
tiles of (approximate) size ε̃(1) × ε(10) can be guaranteed to “span across”99
the edges σ1 of S2 of binary type 10, see Figure 14(e).
    In order to construct the faithful ZSH blueprint B2ff we will need to make
similar additional subdivisions, and impose similar additional conditions. We
are in a two-dimensional case, and therefore the additional subdivisions and
conditions will be based on information from the three-dimensional x1 -x3 -
subdivision S3 , and ZSH pre-blueprint pB3 of S3 .
    In this case there will be not just one, but four binary types100 of faces
σ ∈ S3 for which we have to make sure that corresponding three-dimensional
tiles can span across101 σ.
    We will write down all these conditions systematically, by imposing for
each such binary type that we have

                              length ≫ width ≫ height

for each corresponding three-dimensional tile102 .
  99
      By “span across” we meant that, for any such σ1 , we did not want the two vertical
sides of these rectangular tiles to intersect the edge σ1 , even though the two horizontal
sides do intersect σ1 , as discussed in the previous subsection.
  100
      In the previous case we only had to worry about σ of type 10, because this was the only
type of face σ of S2 that projected via π2 onto a face σ ′ of S1 such that dim σ = dim σ ′ .
(Equal dimensions means that we have to worry about spanning across.) In the case of
S3 there are four types of faces σ of S3 that project via π3 onto a face σ ′ of S2 such that
dim σ = dim σ ′ . These are the faces of type 110, 100, 010, and 000.
  101
      These three-dimensional tiles need to project via π3 on the two-dimensional tiles that
we are constructing now. Therefore, the dimensions of two of the three sides of any such
three-dimensional tile come from the dimensions of the two sides of the two-dimensional
tiles of the faithful ZSH blueprint B2ff , which is now under construction.
  102
      The rigorous meaning of “≫” here is similar to the previous case: we mean that there
exists some ε̃0 < 1 which depends only on S3 and pB3 , such that we have ε̃20 length >
ε̃0 width > height. This makes sense if we also note that we will use these order-of-
magnitude conditions only in statements of the form “if ξ1 ≫ ξ2 then...”, which is a short
and convenient way of expressing the rigorous statement “there exists some ε̃0 < 1 such
that, if ε̃0 ξ1 > ξ2 then...”.




                                             66
Then the conditions are the following:

               For σ ∈ S3 of type 110 :       ε(110) ≫ ε̃(11) ≫ ε̃(1)       (16)
               For σ ∈ S3 of type 100 :       ε(100) ≫ ε(10) ≫ ε̃(1)
               For σ ∈ S3 of type 010 :       ε(010) ≫ ε̃(01) ≫ ε(0)
               For σ ∈ S3 of type 000 :       ε(000) ≫ ε(00) ≫ ε(0)

Note that we have emphasized in (16) the new tile sizes ε̃(11), ε̃(01), and
ε̃(1) using bold fonts; all the other numbers in (16) are values of the form
ε(α) that come from the ZSH pre-blueprint pB3 of S3 .
Let us make two observations about imposing the restrictions (16).
    Our first observation is that these restrictions are already compatible with
the properties of pB3 . Indeed, recall that for any n-dimensional pre-blueprint
p
 Bn we have
                          ε(α1 ...αi ) = ε(α1 ...αi 11...1),
where the binary word α1 ...αi 11...1 has n letters. Also recall that if α and β
are two binary words of n letters which, regarded as binary numbers, satisfy
α < β, then we have
                                 ε(α) ≫ ε(β).
Therefore, if the binary word α1 ...αi is a strict prefix of a binary word of the
form α1′ ...αj′ 0, then we have

                           ε(α1′ ...αj′ 0) ≫ ε(α1 ...αi ),

which are exactly the types of inequalities of the form ε(α) ≫ ε(β) that
appear in (16).
    Our second observation is that we can choose the new numbers ε̃(α) such
that they satisfy the conditions (16). While this two-dimensional case is
quite simple, a general way to do it (which works in the n-dimensional case)
is to proceed in two steps: in a first step define the new numbers ε̃(α1 ...αi 1)
such that the n-dimensional analogue of (16) is almost satisfied, but some
“≫” are actually “=”; and in a second step modify all the numbers where
we have “=” to obtain “≫”, while the previously attained “≫” still holds.
This will be discussed in detail in the next subsection.

    Let us also make one more remark: once we have chosen the numbers
ε̃(1), ε̃(01), and ε̃(11) such that they satisfy (16), here is how we use them.

                                         67
First, as we discussed in the previous subsection, the number ε̃(1) will be
used in the construction of the faithful ZSH blueprint B1ff of S1 . (Recall that
we have used the number ε̃(1) to specify (to an arbitrarily good approxi-
mation) the dimension along the x1 -axis of the tiles of f -nbhd (σ1 ), for any
one-dimensional face σ1 ∈ S1 .
    Then the numbers ε̃(01) and ε̃(11) will be used in the construction of the
faithful ZSH blueprint B2ff of S2 , as follows. The number ε̃(01) will be used
to specify the (approximate) dimension along the x2 -axis of the tiles of f -
nbhd (σ1 ), for any one-dimensional face σ1 ∈ S2 to binary type 01. Similarly,
the number ε̃(11) will be used to specify the (approximate) dimension along
the x2 -axis of the tiles of f -nbhd (σ2 ), for any two-dimensional face σ2 ∈ S2
to binary type 11.
    Of course, as we have mentioned earlier, we could have done much less
work in order to obtain just some ZSH blueprint B2 of S2 . The key point
here is that once we have a faithful ZSH blueprint B2 of S2 , then, by defi-
nition, everything is “prearranged” to allow us to construct a ZSH blueprint
B3 of S3 , and most importantly, to construct a faithful ZSH blueprint B3 of
S3 , and therefore to keep this inductive process going and reach any desired
dimension n.
    Note also that as the dimension increases we do actually impose additional
conditions on the numbers ε̃(α1 ...αi 1) which we have already used in previous
construction steps. For example, when we wanted B1ff to be faithful we
imposed the restriction
                                   ε(10) ≫ ε̃(1),
on ε̃(1), but when we additionally wanted B2ff to be faithful we imposed the
additional restriction
                               ε(110) ≫ ε̃(1)
on ε̃(1), which was not needed in order for B1ff to be faithful, but was needed
in order for B2ff to be faithful. Therefore, we will see that there are different
degrees of faithfulness, and in this case B1ff is not just faithful, but it is 2-
faithful103 .

 103
    In general, if a k-dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint Bkff satisfies the conditions re-
quired for the construction (using the approach that we are discussing here) of an ℓ-
dimensional faithful ZSH blueprint Bℓff (with k < ℓ), then we say that Bkff is ℓ-faithful. In
other words, in order for Bkff to be ℓ-faithful we have to check conditions similar to (16)
up to dimension ℓ + 1. See the next subsection for more details.


                                             68
7.4.3    The n-dimensional case
In this subsection we discuss the general n-dimensional case of our construc-
tion of a faithful ZSH blueprint Bnff for an x1 -xn -subdivision Sn . Our set-
ting will be the following: we will assume that, for the x1 -xi -subdivisions
S1 , ..., Si , ..., Sn , Sn+1 we have already constructed a “chain” of ZHS pre-
blueprints pB1 , pB2 , ..., pBn , pBn+1 , and a “chain” of n-faithful ZSH blueprints
B1ff , B2ff , ..., Bn−1
                     ff
                          , respectively, where we have
                                                      ff
                 Si−1 = πi (Si ), pBi−1 = πi (pBi ), Bj−1 = πj (Bjff ),

for all integers i, j such that 2 ≤ i ≤ n + 1 and 2 ≤ j ≤ n − 1.

Remark. As we have mentioned in previous subsections, the reason we
need faithful ZSH blueprints is the following. First of all, not every (n − 1)-
dimensional ZSH blueprint Bn−1 of the x1 -xn−1 -subdivision Sn−1 = πn (Sn )
can serve as an induction hypothesis for the construction of a n-dimensional
ZSH blueprint Bn for the x1 -xn -subdivision Sn such that Bn−1 = πn (Bn ). On
                    ff
the other hand, if Bn−1 is an n-faithful ZSH blueprint for Sn−1 , then not only
                                                                ff
can we build a ZSH blueprint Bn of Sn such that πn (Bn ) = Bn−1    , but also104
                                                                            ff
we can build a faithful ZSH blueprint Bnff for Sn that is also based on Bn−1   .
Therefore, since n was arbitrary, we can extend this construction of faithful
ZSH blueprints by induction.

    Similar to the previous subsection, our construction will proceed in two
steps. In Step 1 we will just construct a ZSH blueprint Bn for Sn (not yet a
faithful ZSH blueprint). Then, in Step 2, we will further refine our construc-
tion to obtain a faithful ZSH blueprint Bnff .

    Before we start Step 1, let us first discuss the numbers ε̃(α) that will
be needed in our construction, and their relationships to the numbers ε(β)
that are provided to us by the previously constructed “chain” of ZHS pre-
blueprints pB1 , pB2 , ..., pBn , pBn+1 .
    Recall the conditions (16) we discussed in the previous subsection. It was
not difficult to see that all these conditions can be enforced; on the other

     As we have seen in the previous subsection, for this second part we will need to impose

On the other hand, all these conditions simply say that, if we remove the

 105
       Recall where these conditions are coming from: we want to construct B3ff which is a

construction of a blueprint diagram B4 for S4 such that π4 (B4 ) = B3ff . Moreover, if σ ∈ S4
has binary type α1 α2 α3 0, then we want the set f -nbhd (σ) of B4 to approximate the set

f -nbhd (σ) must have length along the x4 -axis be exactly ε(α1 α2 α3 0). Then, in order to be
sure that we can enforce all these restrictions, we have decided to impose conditions on B3ff
which will guarantee that any three-dimensional tile T3 ∈ B3ff allows us to construct four-

the sizes of tiles of B3ff . More precisely, if a tile of B3ff is part of f -nbhd (σ) of some σ ∈ S3
of binary type α1 α2 α3 , and we denote by “∆xi ” the length of T3 along the xi -axis, then
we require that we have ε(α1 α2 α3 0) ≫ ∆x3 ≫ ∆x2 ≫ ∆x1 . When we write down these
requirements for all possible binary words α1 α2 α3 we obtain exactly the conditions (17).

must be much smaller.
   Therefore, in the general n-dimensional case, all the inequalities that
involve some ε̃(α) can be summarized simply as

  ε(α1 ...αj 011...10) ≫ ε̃(α1 ...αj 011...1) ≫ ... ≫ ε̃(α1 ...αj 01) ≫ ε(α1 ...αj 0) (18)

for any binary “prefix” α1 ...αi 0 such that the word α1 ...αj 011...10 above has
at most n + 1 letters107 .
    Moreover, the same inequalities can be summarized in an even simpler
way108 , as

  ε(α1 ...αj 011...10) ≫ ε̃(α1 ...αj 011...1) ≫ ... ≫ ε̃(α1 ...αj 01) ≫ ε(α1 ...αj 0) (19)

for any binary “prefix” α1 ...αi 0 such that the word α1 ...αj 011...10 above has
exactly n + 1 letters109 .
    We will now show that the inequalities (19) can be simultaneously satis-
fied. Indeed, recall how in the previous section we defined110

                           ε(α1 ...αi 011...11) := ε(α1 ...αi 0),

where we obtained the word α1 ...αi 011...11 by adding a sufficient number of
1’s at the end of the word α1 ...αi 0 to make it have maximal length (which
was n in our discussion in the previous section, but it is n+1 here). Our plan
now is to try to use a similar idea111 in order to define ε̃(α1 ...αi 1) for words
 107
      The reason the conditions (18) allow us to address the definition of ε̃(α1) for all the
binary words of interest (i.e., all the words that end with an “1”) is the following: (i) we
only need to define ε̃(α1) for words α1 of length n or less; and (ii) the word “α1 ...αj 0”
above is allowed to be the empty word, in which case we replace “ε(α1 ...αj 0)” by “0” above
(this lets us cover the case of ε̃(11...1) for words “11...1” of length from 1 to n).
  108
      A useful difference between (19) and (18) is that in the set of inequalities (19) each
ε̃(α1 ...αj 011...1) appears only once.
  109
      This is because we already know that, if a word of the form α1 ...αj 011...110 has a
longer sequence of 1’s (denoted “11...11”) than the shorter word α1 ...αj 011...10, then we
have ε(α1 ...αj 011...110) ≫ ε(α1 ...αj 011...10).
  110
      Recall that in the previous section, when discussing n-dimensional ZSH pre-blueprints,
at first we only considered ε(α) for binary words α that ended in a zero; but then it became
convenient to define ε(α) for all binary words α of length exactly n (with the exception of
the word “11...1”).
  111
      But now we do this “in opposite direction”, i.e., now we try to extend the definition

words; in the previous section its was the other way around.


                                             71
that end with “1”; we will see that this almost solves the problem raised by
the inequalities (19), and then we will make one more adjustment in order
to solve it fully.
Indeed, let us first (temporarily) define

                         ε̃(α1 ...αi 1) := ε(α1 ...αi 111...11),

where, like above, we added a sufficient number of 1’s at the end of the word
α1 ...αi 1 to make it have length n + 1.
     Then, if we check the inequalities (19), we will see that they are “almost”
satisfied, except we actually have

                             ε̃(α1 ...αi 11) = ε̃(α1 ...αi 1),

because when we add a sufficient number of 1’s at the end of the word
α1 ...αi 11, and also add a sufficient number of 1’s at the end of the word
α1 ...αi 1, we actually obtain the same word of length n+1. Therefore, instead
of (19) we actually have

  ε(α1 ...αj 011...10) ≫ ε̃(α1 ...αj 011...1) = ... = ε̃(α1 ...αj 01) = ε(α1 ...αj 0),

where the word “α1 ...αj 011...10” has exactly n + 1 letters, and the common
prefix “α1 ...αj 0” may also be the empty word, in which case we replace
ε(α1 ...αj 0) by “0”.
   Then, since “there is enough space” between the order of magnitude of
ε(α1 ...αj 011...10) and the order of magnitude of ε(α1 ...αj 0), we can now
modify all the values ε̃(α1 ...αj 01), ..., ε̃(α1 ...αj 011...1) to impose that we have

  ε(α1 ...αj 011...10) ≫ ε̃(α1 ...αj 011...1) ≫ ... ≫ ε̃(α1 ...αj 01) ≫ ε(α1 ...αj 0),

and we obtain a solution for the inequalities (19).

a face σ ∈ Sn intersects a tile Tn ⊂ f −nbhd (σ0 ) if and only if the basepoint
of Tn belongs to σ. But then σ intersects the relative interior of σ0 , which
implies that σ0 ⊂ σ; moreover, if σ0 ̸= σ then it implies σ0 ⊂ ∂σ.

Therefore, we obtain the following:

8      Proof of the global attractor conjecture in
       the n-dimensional case
Consider some toric dynamical system Tn in Rn>0 . As we discussed in pre-
vious sections, we embed Tn into a toric differential inclusion Tn , and we
already know that, if we can construct an exhaustive family of ZSH for Tn ,
then we obtain a proof of the global attractor conjecture.
    We know that we can construct a ZSH blueprint Bn for Tn . After that,
our plan is the following: (Step 1) explain how to convert Bn into the kind
of “restricted ZSH blueprint” denoted BnP , whose tiles are contained in the
set DnP , such that BnP can be used for the construction of ZSH117 for Tn , and
(Step 2) explain how we can use BnP for the construction of an exhaustive
family of ZSH for Tn . We now discuss these two steps, in this order.

Step 1. Recall that, when we constructed a (say, two-dimensional) ZSH
blueprint B2 in section 7, we did not restrict its tiles to the set D2P , which
(up to identifying R2 with the affine plane {X1 = 1} of R3 ) was the com-
pactification of the set
                        {(X2P , X3P ) ∈ R2 |1 ≤ X2P ≤ X3P },
but when we discussed two-dimensional ZSH blueprints in Section 6 (where
we actually used these blueprint to construct two-dimensional polyhedral
ZSH), all the tiles of a ZSH blueprint were contained inside D2P (for example,
see Figure 4 (b)).
    Note though that the boundary rays of D2P are faces of the subdivision
  P
F2 . Then there is a very simple way to convert an already constructed ZSH
blueprint B2 that is defined on the whole R2 (for an x1 -x2 -subdivision S2
that contains the faces of a given subdivision subdivision F2P of D2P ), into a
“restricted ZSH blueprint” B2P whose tiles are contained in D2P : for each tile
T2 of B2 whose interior intersects D2P we define a tile T2P of B2P given by
                                  T2P = T2 ∩ D2P .
Also, we define the basepoint of T2P to be the same as the basepoint of
T2 . Note that, since the two boundary rays of D2P are union of faces of the
 117
    Recall that, when we used a ZSH blueprint B2 to construct ZSH in 3D, the blueprint
B2 was restricted to the set D2P , or equivalently, was restricted to the set D2H .


                                         77
subdivision F2P , it follows that if a tile T2P intersects the boundary of D2P
then the basepoint of T2P lies on the boundary of D2P (see Figure 4, Figure 9,
and Figure 14 for examples.).
   Also, in order to obtain exactly the kind of two-dimensional ZSH blueprint
that we have used in Section 6, we need to also intersect all the tiles T2P with
a “blue box” of the form
                               [0, M3 ] × [0, M2 ],
for M3 ≫ M2 ≫ 1, to obtain all the bounded tiles of B2P 118 .
    Finally, in order to finish the construction of B2P , we need to construct the
“boundary tiles” of B2P (see Figure 10(a)). For this, we choose tile vertices
Vi along the sides of the blue box where we have {X3 = M3 } or {X2 = M2 },
in such a way that, when we draw rays that connect the origin to each Vi ,
the rays separate the slopes of rays contained within the subdivision S2 119 .
    The two-dimensional case discussed above suggests the following process
for the transition from our construction of a “global” ZSH blueprint Bn to the
definition of a “restricted” ZSH blueprint denoted BnP , in any dimension. Let

Remark. Recall that the Persistence Conjecture says that any n-dimensional
weakly reversible system is persistent [3]. A stronger version of this conjec-

weakly reversible system is persistent. We obtain the following partial re-

variable-k weakly reversible126 system is persistent.

                                           81
9     Appendix: some general results about fans,
      toric differential inclusions, and ZSH
In this section we discuss some technical results that we used in previous
sections. For some of these results, for the sake of a simpler notation, we
formulate and prove them in 3D instead of nD; the proof in nD is analogous.

9.1    Finer and coarser fans, embeddings of toric differ-
       ential inclusions, forward invariant regions
The following definition clarifies what we mean by “the fan F1 is coarser than
the fan F2 ”, or equivalently, “the fan F2 is finer than the fan F1 ”.

Definition 9.1. Given two fans F1 and F2 in Rn , we say that F2 is finer than F1
(or F1 is coarser than F2 ) if any cone in F1 can be written as a union of
cones in F2 .

    We now want to show that forward invariant regions of toric differential
inclusions generated by the finer fan are also forward invariant regions of
toric differential inclusions generated by the coarser fan; for this we need the
notion of “embedding” for differential inclusions.

Definition 9.2. Given two differential inclusions dx dt
                                                        ∈ F1 (x) and dxdt
                                                                          ∈
F2 (x), we say that the first one is embedded in the second one if F1 (x) ⊆
F2 (x) for all x.

    The following lemma and its corollary allow us to replace a toric differ-
ential inclusion T1 with a more convenient one (denoted T2 ) and argue that
ZSH for the new toric differential inclusion are actually also ZSH for the old
toric differential inclusion we started with.

Lemma 9.3. Consider a number δ > 0 and two fans F1 and F2 in Rn such
that F2 is finer than F1 . If T1 is the toric differential inclusion generated by
(F1 , δ), and T2 is the toric differential inclusion generated by (F2 , δ), then T1
is embedded in T2 .

Proof. Consider some x ∈ Rn>0 . For each cone K1 ∈ F1 at distance < δ from
the point log(x), there exists some cone K2 ∈ F2 that is also at distance < δ



                                        82
from the point log(x), such that K2 ⊆ K1 . But this implies that the polars
of these two cones satisfy K1o ⊆ K2o , so we obtain

                         FF1 ,δ (log(x)) ⊆ FF2 ,δ (log(x)),

i.e., T1 is embedded in T2 .
   Lemma 9.3 immediately implies the following result.

Corollary 9.4. Consider a number δ > 0 and two fans F1 and F2 in Rn
such that F2 is finer than F1 . Denote by T1 the toric differential inclusion
generated by (F1 , δ), and by T2 the toric differential inclusion generated by
(F2 , δ). Assume that T2 cannot cross some surface Z within a set Ω ⊂ Rn .
Then T1 also cannot cross Z within Ω.



9.2    Necessary and sufficient conditions for ZSH
Consider a ZSH denoted Z inside the unit cube (0, 1)3 , and recall that we
can assume that the normal line at any smooth point of Z is contained in
the union of the (closed) positive orthant and the (closed) negative orthant.
The outer normal of Z at a point x ∈ Z is defined as the normal direction
of Z at x pointing into the (closed) negative orthant. Then we have:

Lemma 9.5. Consider a toric differential inclusion T3 in R3>0 with polyhedral
fan F3 and assume that a piecewise smooth surface Z is a ZSH for T3 and
is contained in the unit cube (0, 1)3 . Then, for any point x ∈ Z where Z is
smooth we have: if C ∈ F3 is a polyhedral cone such that log(x) ∈ C, then
the outer normal vector of the surface Z at the point x must belong to the
cone C.

Proof. Since Z is a zero-separating surface for T3 and log(x) ∈ C, it follows
that the tangent plane to Z at x is a supporting plane of the polar cone C o
(otherwise the cone C o would provide a way for trajectories of T3 to “cross
through” the zero-separating surface Z at x). Therefore, the outer normal of
Z at x must belong to the polar cone of C o . In conclusion, the outer normal
of Z at x belongs to the polar of the polar of the cone C, which is simply
C.


                                        83
Remark 9.6. Lemma 9.5 provides a very convenient necessary condition that
any ZSH Z should satisfy: its outer normal direction at any (smooth) point
x must belong to a cone of F3 that is easy to specify, because it is exactly
the cone that contains the point log(x). If several cones C ∈ F3 contain
the point log(x), then we obtain more information from this lemma if we
select the smallest such cone. Most importantly for us, this lemma provides
a geometric condition for Z that does not involve polar cones any more; it
only involves cones from the polyhedral fan F3 .
   We will see below that this necessary condition can be modified to obtain
a very useful sufficient condition.
Lemma 9.7. Consider a toric differential inclusion T3 in R3>0 given by a
fan127 F3 and a fixed number δ > 0. Assume that for any cone C ∈ F3≤ we
are able to specify a cone KC ⊂ {X3 ≤ X2 ≤ X1 ≤ 0} such that C is contained
in the relative interior of KC with respect to the set {X3 ≤ X2 ≤ X1 ≤ 0},
and the property below is satisfied:
    For any ε̂ > 0 there exists a piecewise smooth surface Zε̂ such that
    (i) Zε̂ ⊂ (0, 1)3 \ (ε̂ + [0, 1]3 )
and
    (ii) for any smooth point P ∈ Zε̂ we have: if log(P ) ∈ KC , then there is
a normal vector ⃗nP of Zε̂ at P such that128 ⃗nP ∈ C.
Then, for any ε̂ small enough, T3 cannot cross Zε̂ within (0, 1)3 .
Proof. Consider some C ∈ F3≤ . We need to show that for any ε̂ small enough
the following is true: if a point P ∈ Zε̂ satisfies

                                   log(P ) ∈ B(C, δ),

where B(C, δ) is defined as the set of points at distance at most δ from C,
then there exists a normal vector of Zε̂ at P that belongs to C.
    Note first the following remark: for any cones C1 , C2 ⊂ Rn such that C1
is contained in the interior of C2 , it follows that there exists some number
M > 0 such that we have

                              B(C1 , δ) \ B(0, M ) ⊂ C2 ,
 127
     Recall that we are assuming that our fans are x1 -x2 -x3 -symmetric and contain the
planes xi = xj and xi = 0.
 128
     We will refer to this ⃗nP as “the outer normal” of Zε̂ at P . Note that ⃗nP belongs to
the (closed) negative orthant of R3 .


                                            84
i.e., all the points of B(C1 , δ) that lie outside the ball of radius MC must
belong to KC .129
     Note now that since C is contained in the relative interior of KC with
respect to the set {X3 ≤ X2 ≤ X1 ≤ 0}, it follows that C is contained in the
interior of KCsym , where KCsym is the union between KC and all its symmetric
“mirror images” within Rn130 .
     Then we can apply the remark above to conclude that there exists some
number MC > 0 such that we have

                              B(C, δ) \ B(0, MC ) ⊂ KCsym .

    Finally, if ε̂ is small enough, it follows that log(P ) lies outside the ball
B(0, MC ), and therefore log(P ) ∈ KCsym ; but we also have log(P ) ∈ {X3 ≤
X2 ≤ X1 ≤ 0}, which implies log(P ) ∈ KC . Then the outer normal ⃗nP of
Zε̂ at P satisfies ⃗nP ∈ C. Now the desired conclusion follows from the fact
that there are only finitely many cones C ∈ F3 , so for ε̂ small enough we can
guarantee that the reasoning above works for all C ∈ F3≤ .


Remark 9.8. Lemma 9.7 is very useful for our process for constructing the
ZSH, because it allows us to “trade” the restriction that ε is very small (which
we need to make anyway) to account for the possibility that δ might be quite
large. More specifically, in practice, it follows that it is sufficient to con-
struct a single “good” ZSH blueprint, and the same blueprint will work for
any (fixed) δ; for larger δ we just need to start the construction of the ZSH
(for the same ZSH blueprint) with a smaller ε.


 129
     Geometrically, we could formulate it like this: if we look outside a big enough
sphere centered at the origin, then the “constant width neighborhood” B(C1 , δ) of C1 will
be contained inside the “growing width neighborhood” C2 of C1 . A short proof of this
fact follows from the observation that dist(C1 ∩ B(0, 1), ∂C2 ) > 0, which implies that
dist(C1 ∩ B(0, M ), ∂C2 ) > δ for large enough M .
 130
     This is because C sym is contained in the interior of KCsym and, of course, C is contained
in C sym .

9.3    Restrictions of ΨP3 , and images of straight line seg-

Consider the function ΨP3 : (0, 1)3 → R2>0 given by

    We show that if we restrict ΨP3 to an affine planes near the origin, and
if this affine plane “cuts off” the corner of the positive orthant, then the
restriction is a diffeomorphism:
Lemma 9.9. Consider an affine plane π that intersects the positive orthant
and has a normal vector inside the negative orthant. If the distance between
the origin and π is small enough, then the restriction of
                                                         
                       P                    log x2 log x3
                     Ψ3 (x1 , x2 , x3 ) =         ,

to π, i.e., the map
                           ΨP3            : π ∩ R3>0 → R2 ,
                                 π∩R3>0

is a diffeomorphism between π ∩ R3>0 and its image via ΨP3 .
Proof. We just need to check that the restricted map is injective and that it is
locally a diffeomorphism (i.e., its Jacobian is not singular anywhere). These
can both be verified using elementary calculations. For example, injectivity
follows if we write the plane as

                             a1 x1 + a2 x2 + a3 x3 = b,

for some ai ≥ 0 (not all zero) and some b > 0, and note that for any u, v > 0
the curve t → (t, tu , tv ) intersects this plane for at most (and actually exactly)
one value t0 ∈ (0, 1). This also shows that we can allow the normal vector to
lie on the boundary of the negative orthant, as long as we further restrict the
domain to be the set π ∩(0, 1)3 . Also, we don’t even need the hypothesis that
π is very close to the origin; it is actually sufficient that π ∩ (0, 1)3 ̸= ∅.


Next, we analyze the slopes of images of straight lines near the origin of R3>0 ,
via the map ΨP3 .

                                  t
Then, for example, in case (i) we want to show that
                      −v1 t1−X + v3 X ≫ | − v2 t1−Y + v3 Y |.
This follows if we take into account that, for small a enough neighborhood
Vε1 ,ε2 (i.e., if t is small enough), the hypotheses X − Y > ε1 , Y − 1 > ε1 imply
t1−X ≫ t1−Y , t1−X ≫ X, t1−Y ≫ Y , which imply
                      −v1 t1−X ≫ | − v2 t1−Y + v3 Y | + |v3 X|.
The other cases are similar.



                                            88
9.4     Asymptotic level sets of the Horn-Jackson Lya-
        punov function
Consider a Horn-Jackson Lyapunov function V : Rn>0 → R given by
                                         n
                                        X          xi
                    V (x1 , ..., xn ) =     (xi log 0 − xi + x0i ),
                                        i=1
                                                   xi

for some fixed (x01 , ..., x0n ) ∈ Rn>0 . Then we have:

Lemma 9.11. For large values of M , the level set of the Horn-Jackson
Lyapunov function given by the equation

                                   V (x1 , ..., xn ) = M,

is contained between two simplicial sets of the form
                             n                             
                             X                       C
                                   xi = α 1 ±
                             i=1
                                                   log M

for some value α ∼ M/log(M ) and for some for some constant C > 0 that
depends only on n.

Proof. The proof of this lemma follows from elementary considerations. For
example we can calculate the minimum      of V and the maximum of V along
an arbitrary simplex of the form ni=1 xi = α. for large values of α. (The
                                   P
minimum is attained at a point xmin that is proportional with the vector x0
that shows up in the expression of V , and the maximum is attained at a point
xmax where all but one of the coordinates are zero; the nonzero coordinate
of xmax is the one where x0 has its smallest coordinate.)
